title: Commentary on the Golden Verses
author: Hierocles

lines.text: The Golden Verses of the Pythagoreans

First honour the immortal gods, as they are ordered by law, and revere the oath. Next, the illustrious heroes; and venerate the terrestrial daemons, performing what is lawful. Honour your parents too, and those most nearly related to you. Of all others, make him your friend who is best in virtue.

Yield to gentle words and to helpful deeds, and do not hate your friend for a small fault, so far as you are able; for ability dwells close to necessity. Know these things so; and accustom yourself to master these: the belly first of all, and sleep, and lust,

and anger. Never do anything shameful, either with another or by yourself; and above all, feel shame before yourself. Next, practise justice in deed and in word, and do not accustom yourself to act thoughtlessly in anything; but know that death is appointed for all,

and that wealth is wont now to be gained, now to be lost. Of all the pains that mortals suffer by divine fortunes, whatever lot you have, bear it gently and do not chafe at it. Yet it is fitting to heal it as far as you can; and consider this: the lot does not give very much of these to the good.

Many words, both base and noble, fall upon men's ears; be not dismayed by them, nor yet let yourself be kept from them. But if some falsehood is spoken, yield gently. And what I tell you now, let it be fulfilled in every case: let no one by word or deed induce you

to do or say what is not best for you. Deliberate before the deed, lest it turn out foolish; to do and say senseless things is the mark of a wretched man. But do those things that will not grieve you afterward. Do nothing that you do not understand, but learn

what is needful; and so you will lead a most delightful life. Nor should you be careless of the body's health, but keep measure in drink and food and exercise; and by measure I mean what will not grieve you. Accustom yourself to a way of life that is clean and unpampered,

and guard against doing such things as bring envy. Do not spend out of season, like one ignorant of what is noble, nor be illiberal: measure is best in all things. Do those things that will not harm you, and reason before the deed. Do not let sleep come upon your soft eyes

before you have reckoned over each deed of the day: “Where did I transgress? What did I do? What duty did I leave undone?” Begin from the first and go through them all; and then, if you have done base things, rebuke yourself; if good things, rejoice. Labour at these things, practise them; these you must love;

these will set you in the footsteps of divine virtue — yes, by him who handed down to our soul the Tetraktys, fount of ever-flowing nature. But go to your work, having prayed to the gods to bring it to completion. Having mastered these, you will know the constitution of immortal gods and mortal men,

how each thing is distinguished and how it is held together; you will know, as is right, that nature is in all things alike, so that you will neither hope for what is not to be hoped, nor will anything escape you. You will know men whose sufferings are self-chosen, wretched, who, though good things are near, neither see

nor hear them; and few understand the release from evils. Such is the lot that harms the minds of mortals: like cylinders they roll now here, now there, suffering endless woes. For baneful Strife, their inborn companion, harms them unnoticed; one must not provoke it, but yield and flee.

Father Zeus, surely you would free all men from many evils, if you showed to all what daemon they make use of. But take courage, for mortals are of divine race, to whom sacred Nature, bringing all things forth, reveals each one. If you have any share in these, you will master what I command you,

and, healing your soul, you will save it from these toils. But abstain from the foods we spoke of, in the purifications and in the release of the soul, judging each thing; and consider all, setting above you, as charioteer, the best judgment. And if, leaving the body behind, you come to the free aether,
you will be immortal, a god undying, no longer mortal.
The Commentary
Proem

Philosophy is the purification and perfection of human life: purification from material irrationality and from the mortal-formed body, and perfection as the recovery of our proper well-being, leading us back to likeness to God. These two things, virtue and truth, are best fitted by nature to accomplish: virtue by banishing the immoderation of the passions, truth by bestowing the divine form on those who are naturally disposed to receive it.

For this science, then, which is to make us pure and perfect, we need certain rules, briefly defined, like the aphorisms of an art, so that by their means we may arrive methodically and in due order at the goal of well-being. And among such rules as bear upon the whole of philosophy, we may with good reason give the first place to the Pythagorean verses that are called "golden". For they contain the general doctrines of all philosophy, both practical and contemplative, by means of which one may acquire truth and virtue, recover oneself pure, and be fortunate enough to attain likeness to God; and, as Plato's Timaeus says — that exact teacher of the Pythagorean doctrines — having become healthy and whole, one may arrive at the form of one's former state.

And first the Verses set out the precepts of practical virtue. For we must first bring into order the irrationality and indolence within us, and only then apply ourselves to the knowledge of divine things. For just as an eye that is inflamed and not cleansed cannot look upon things of great brightness, so a soul that has not acquired virtue cannot behold the beauty of truth as in a mirror; for it is not lawful for the impure to touch the pure.

Practical philosophy is productive of virtue, contemplative philosophy of truth; and so in the Verses themselves we find practical philosophy called human virtue, and contemplative philosophy celebrated as divine virtue. For, having concluded the precepts of civic virtue, the discourse says:
45 Labour at these things, practise them; these you must love; 46 these will set you in the footsteps of divine virtue.

We must, therefore, first become men, and then gods. The civic virtues make a man good; the sciences that lead up to divine virtue make him a god. Now for those who ascend, the lesser things come in order before the greater; and this is why, in the Pythagorean precepts, the discourse delivers the precepts of the virtues first in the Verses, training us to rise from the best use of the things of this life to likeness to God. This, then, is the aim and the order of the Verses: to set before those who hear them the character of the philosopher, before all other readings.

They received the name "golden" because, as verses go, they are the best and most divine. So too we call the best among the races of men the "golden race", taking the difference of characters from the analogy of the metals. For gold is something unadulterated and not filled with earth, as are the metals akin to it and next after it, such as silver, bronze and iron, which are so filled; and over these gold has a natural superiority, since it alone of them breeds no rust, whereas each of the others turns to rust in proportion as it partakes of earth. Since, then, earthy rust is taken to stand for material vice, the holy and pure race, and the character wholly clean of wickedness, was fittingly called golden; and in the same way these verses, being beautiful through and through, have been given the title "golden" and divine. For it is not that one part of them is beautiful and another not, as with some other poems; rather all of them alike display the pure character, lead up to likeness to God, and unveil the most perfect aim of the Pythagorean philosophy, as will become clear in the exposition of each verse in turn. And first let us begin with the first.
I · Verse 1
1 First honour the immortal gods, as they are ordered by law,

Since piety, which has its reference to the divine cause, is the leader of all the virtues, the precept concerning it rightly stands at the head of the laws laid down in the Verses: namely, that we must honour the gods within the cosmos according to the order inherent in them, which the demiurgic law brought forth together with their very being, placing some of them in the first sphere, others in the second, others again in the third, and so on in succession until the whole number of the heavenly circles is complete. For to know and honour them in the rank in which they were ordered by their Demiurge and Father is the part of those who follow the divine law and render them true honour. And neither to exalt their dignity beyond measure nor to fall short of it in our conceptions of them, but to hold that they are what they have come to be, and have the rank they have been allotted, carries our reverence up to God their Demiurge, whom one might properly call the God of gods, God supreme and best.

We shall discover the true dignity of the world-making God, the best of craftsmen, only if we regard him as the cause of gods and the maker of unchangeable rational beings. For those whom the discourse here names "immortal gods" are those who always and in the same way think the Demiurgic God, who are ever intent upon his good, and who receive from him their being and their well-being indivisibly and unchangeably, as impassive images of the demiurgic cause, untouched by evil. For it befits God to establish such images of himself as well, and not all of them changeable and subject to passion through a leaning toward vice, as are human souls, which are the lowest class of rational natures, just as, conversely, the class now called "the immortal gods" is the highest.

And perhaps these were called "immortal gods" by way of distinction from human souls, because they never die to the divine well-being, nor ever fall into forgetfulness either of their own essence or of the Father's goodness. But the human soul is subject to these affections: at one time it thinks God and recovers its own dignity, at another it falls away from both. Hence human souls might fittingly be called mortal gods, since they at times die to the divine well-being by fleeing from God, and come to life in it again by turning back to God; and so in the one condition they live the divine life, and in the other they die — so far as an immortal essence can have a share in the lot of death — not by passing into non-being, but by falling away from well-being. For the death of a rational being is godlessness and folly, on which follows the uprising of the passions, beyond all measure, in its life. For in ignorance of what is better one must be a slave to what is worse; and from this slavery there is no release except by turning back, through recollection, to intellect and to God.

Between those called immortal gods and those we have called mortal gods there must be some class, more honourable than man but inferior to a god, which through its own middle position links the extremes to one another, so that the whole of the rational creation may be well bound together with itself. This middle class never has a complete ignorance of God, nor yet a knowledge wholly immovable and abiding always the same; it always knows, but apprehends now in one way, now in another, sometimes more and sometimes less. By always knowing it rises above the human race; by not knowing unchangeably and always in the same way it falls below the divine. It is a mean by nature; it was neither raised from man to the middle rank by progress, nor sunk to it from the rank of god by neglect.

For the Demiurgic God established first, second and third natures, differing from one another by nature, not confused with one another, and not exchanging their rank through virtue and vice. These, standing eternally in their essence, were distinguished by kind according to the order that came forth together with them, and were ordered in proportion to the demiurgic causes. For as there, in the all-perfect wisdom, the order holds of first, middle and last — for this is the very being of wisdom, to bring forth its making in order and perfection, so that wisdom, order and perfection go together — so too in this universe the beings that came to be according to the first thoughts of God would be first in the cosmos, those according to his middle thoughts would themselves be middle, and those resembling the limit of his thoughts would be last among rational beings. For the whole rational order, together with the incorruptible body connate with it, is an image of the whole Demiurgic God. The first beings in the cosmos are an undefiled image of the summit there; the middle beings here are a middle image of the middle there; and the third and last among rational beings are a last image of the limit of the divinity there. Of these three classes, the present discourse has signified the first by "immortal gods", the middle by "illustrious heroes", and the last by "terrestrial daemons", as we shall see a little later.

But now let us return to where we began. What is the law, what is the order that accords with it, and what is the honour rendered in keeping with that order? Law is the demiurgic intellect and the divine will, which brings forth all things eternally and preserves them for ever. Lawful order is that which, from the Father and Demiurge of all, entered into being together with the immortal gods, and makes some of them first, others second. For although, within the whole rational order, they have been allotted the summit, they are nonetheless diversified among themselves, and some are more divine than others. A mark of their superiority and subordination in essence is the order of the heavenly spheres, which have received their positions according to essence and power; so that the law lies in their very essence, and their order is of one nature with their dignity. For they did not come into existence at random and afterwards get separated; they proceeded into being already ordered, as different parts of the whole heaven, as of a single living being, preserving their coordination with one another at once in their distinction of kind and in their conjunction; so that no exchange of their positions could ever be conceived except together with the destruction of the universe. And this cannot happen so long as their first cause remains wholly unchangeable and unalterable, possessing an essence identical with its activity, and having goodness not as something acquired but as its very essence, by itself and through itself leading all things to well-being.

For no other reasonable cause of his making of all things can be assigned to him but the goodness that is his essence. "He was good," it says, "and in the good no envy about anything ever arises." The causes of the creation of this universe that are alleged apart from goodness befit human circumstances rather than God. Being good, then, in his essence, God brought forth first by nature the beings most made like himself; second, those possessing a middle likeness to him; and third, and last of all the beings that resemble him, those that fall furthest short of likeness to God. And their order ran together with the essence of the beings that came to be, so that the naturally better is ranked before the inferior, both among the classes taken as wholes and among those that have a gradation of species within each class. For it was not by the allotment of fortune that all things received their rank, nor by changes of choice; they were brought forth different by demiurgic laws, and were allotted an order proportionate to the worth of their natures. Therefore the words "as they are ordered by law, honour" must be understood as applying in common not only to the immortal gods but also to the illustrious heroes and to human souls. For in each class there is a multitude of species ranked by superiority and subordination.

Such, then, is the nature and the order of rational beings. But what is the law, and the honour that follows it? We say again that law is the unchangeable demiurgic activity of God, which begets the divine classes and orders them eternally and immutably; and the honour that accords with the law is knowledge of the essence of those we honour, and likening ourselves to them as far as we can. For what one admires, one also imitates as far as one is able; and one honours him who lacks nothing by receiving the good things that he holds out. For you will not honour God best by giving him something, but by making yourself worthy to receive what comes from him. For, as the Pythagoreans say, "You will honour God best if you make your understanding like God"; and, "Whoever honours God as though he stood in need of anything unwittingly supposes himself to be greater than God"; and, "Costly offerings do not become honour to God unless they are brought with a mind filled with God. For the gifts and sacrifices of fools are fuel for the fire, and their votive offerings a provision for temple-robbers; but a mind filled with God, firmly and lastingly established, joins us to God." For like must needs go to like; and this is why the wise man alone is called a priest, he alone dear to God, he alone knows how to pray. For he alone knows how to honour who does not confound the dignity of those he honours, who first of all offers himself as the victim, who fashions his own soul into a divine statue, and who prepares his own intellect as a temple to receive the divine light. For what can you offer of this kind from the materials lying all around us, that will make a statue congenial to God, or a gift able to be united with him? Yet this must necessarily come about in the rational being once it is purified. For, as the same men say, God has no place on earth more fitting than a pure soul; and with them the Pythian god agrees, saying:
"In pious mortals I delight as much as in Olympus."

The pious man is he who possesses divine knowledge and offers his own perfection as the best honour to the causes of good things; who, in his eagerness to acquire them, turns back to those whose nature it is to bestow them, and who, by being able to receive the good things, honours those who ever give them. But whoever chooses to honour the divine in some other way, and not through himself, makes his honour a mere outlay of outward abundance, offering not a virtue of his own but acquitting himself of the duty with things outside himself. Yet even a good man takes no pleasure in receiving such things unless they are given with the best disposition. Of this kind, again, is the saying of the Pythian god. For when a man who had sacrificed hecatombs without a pious mind asked how his gifts had been received, the god answered:
"But the barley-meal of the renowned man of Hermione pleased me,"

preferring the cheapest offering to all that costliness, because it was adorned by a mind that reveres God. For with this, all things are dear to God; and without it nothing could ever be pleasing to God.

So much, then, has been said sufficiently for the present concerning reverence for God and holiness. But since the law of the ordering of the universe is preserved by an unchangeable guard, and it was the custom of the ancients, in their secret teachings, to call the keeper of this guard "oath", it is fitting that next after what has been said he introduces, as a doctrine that follows from it, the precept concerning the oath.
II · Verse 2
2 and revere the oath.

Law, we declared in what went before, is the activity of God that is always the same, which eternally and unchangeably brings all things forth into being. Oath, accordingly, following upon law, we would now call the cause that keeps all things in sameness and so makes them firm that, held fast as by the faith of an oath, they preserve the order of the law; so that the inviolability of the good order in created things is the effect of the demiurgic law. For that all things abide as they are disposed by law would be the principal work of the divine oath, which in the beings that always think God is preserved in the highest degree and always; but in those that at times think him and at times fall away from the knowledge of God, the oath too is in like manner transgressed by those who fall away, and kept again by those who are led up to the turning back to God. For the keeping of the divine laws is here called oath, by which all things that are by nature able to know the Demiurgic God are bound to him and hang from him; and of these, those that always cleave to him always revere the oath, while those that at some time fall away then also commit impiety against the oath, transgressing not only the order of the divine law but also the faith of the divine oath. Such, then, is the oath that is inherent in the essence of the rational classes, compelling them to cleave to their Father and Maker and never in any way to transgress the laws that he has laid down.

But the oath used in the transactions of life is a trace of that one, directing towards truth those who use it as they ought. For it transforms the wavering of human choice into firmness, and compels it to abide in sameness in both words and deeds, on the one hand bringing to light the clear truth of what has happened, and on the other exacting certainty for what is going to happen.

For these reasons, then, it is especially fitting to revere the oath: the one that pre-exists in essence, because of its guardianship of eternity; the human one, which is a helper in the affairs of life, as the image of the former, and which, next after that one, has become for us the presiding power of firmness and truth, and fills with the noblest habits of character those who have learned to revere it. And the only reverence of an oath would be the unhindered keeping, so far as lies in our power, of what has been sworn — the keeping that, by a voluntary necessity, attunes those who revere the oath to the steadfastness and truthfulness of the divine state.

Now the first and ineffable keeping of the oath is by nature recovered, through turning back to God, by those who, through the purificatory virtues, heal their breach of the divine oath; while the keeping of the oath in life is preserved by the civic virtues. For only those who possess these virtues are able to keep their oaths in the affairs of life also; but vice, the mother of perjury, tramples the oath underfoot through the instability of character. For how could the lover of money ever be true to his oath when he is to receive or repay money? And how would the intemperate man or the coward abide by his oaths? Will not each of them, wherever he thinks he will gain some advantage in the things by which he is overcome, there cast off his reverence for oaths, bartering divine goods for mortal and perishable ones? But in those in whom the possession of the virtues is well established, the reverence of oaths is also naturally well preserved.

The best practice for keeping one's reverence for the oath is not to use the oath frequently, nor at random, nor on chance occasions, nor to fill out a speech, nor to vouch for a story, but, so far as possible, to reserve its use for matters at once necessary and honourable, and then only when no other means of safety in such matters appears except through the truth that comes from the oath alone. And these things will be credible to those who hear us if we show a character in accord with the oath, and leave no suspicion that in human affairs anything could ever seem to us greater than truth, whether we are unsworn or swearing.

So "revere the oath" enjoins not only keeping one's oaths but also abstaining from oaths. For it is thus that we shall keep our oaths true: if we do not abuse oaths. For in continual swearing one may easily slip into perjury, whereas sparing use is followed by keeping. For a man will either not swear, or, when he swears, he will keep his oath; and neither will his tongue run ahead through habit, nor his understanding trip through incontinence of the passions. For the understanding will be set right by his character, being good, and the tongue by the habit of abstaining from swearing.

Keeping one's oath befits the honour of the gods spoken of before, as being always inborn in piety and its attendant; for the oath too, as we saw, was the guardian of the divine law in the ordering of the universe. Honour the law, then, by following its ordinance, and revere the oath by not abusing it lightly, so that you may become accustomed to keep your oaths from not being accustomed to swear. For the keeping of oaths is no small part of piety.

So much concerning the first class of the superior beings, and the divine law that governs their order, and the oath that accompanies the law. Next he adds that the class after the gods also, which we said is the angelic, must be honoured in the second place.
III · Verse 2
2 Next, the illustrious heroes;

These are the middle class of rational beings, who, filling the place next after the immortal gods, rank before human nature and join through themselves the last to the first. To these, then, as second, we must render the second honour, understanding in their case too the words "honour them, as they are ordered by law". For the whole force of honour lies in the knowledge of the essence of those honoured, from which one also discovers well and rightly what it is fitting to say or do towards those who are honoured. For how could anyone converse with those he does not know? And how will he bring a gift to those whose worth he does not know? The first and true honour, then, in the case of the illustrious heroes too, is the knowledge of their essence and rank, and an understanding of the activity that accompanies it and of the contribution it extends to this universe.

In every case the honour must be made commensurate with the essences; and this comes from the science concerning them. For when we have discerned how each thing stands in nature and in rank, then we shall also render them honour in accordance with the law. But we shall honour nothing that is inferior to human being; we shall honour, principally, only the beings superior by nature, and also those equal to us that have been adorned with a pre-eminence of virtue.

Of the beings superior by nature, the first and best is the Demiurgic God, who is honoured incomparably above all. Of the beings in the cosmos, the first are those that are from him and after him, who think him unchangeably and, without being affected, bear the image of the participation in good things that descends upon them from the demiurgic cause. These the present discourse has called immortal gods, because they do not die, nor do they lose their likeness to God, but continue in it always and in the same way.

In the middle in essence and in honour are those now called the illustrious heroes, who always think the Demiurge and are illumined by the well-being that comes from him, but not in the same way nor unchangeably. For, being united to God in a middle degree and admitting of a change that is untouched by vice, they dance about him with now one and now another act of apprehension; and the changeless and unified contemplation of the first beings they both divide and gather together by their own multiplied knowledge, making the limits of the others' epoptic vision the beginnings of their own initiation.

Hence they are fittingly called illustrious heroes: illustrious (agauoi), as being good (agathoi) and ever luminous, and never falling into vice or forgetfulness; heroes (hērōes), as being in a manner loves (erōes), that is, erōtes — erotic and dialectical lovers, as it were, of God — lifting (airontes) us and raising us up from our sojourn on earth to the divine commonwealth. The same beings it is customary to call good daemons too, as being knowing (daēmones) and skilled in the divine laws, and sometimes also angels, as revealing and announcing (diangellontes) to us the rules that lead to well-being.

Often, too, using the three names, we divide the breadth of the middle class into three, and call the part nearest the heavenly beings angels, the part joined to the earthly ones heroes, and the part equally distant from both extremes daemons, as Plato does in many places. But some call the whole middle class by one of the three names, calling them all angels or daemons or heroes, for the reasons we have stated; just as here too he has called the whole middle class illustrious heroes, who stand to the first class as radiance to fire and as a child to a father.

Hence the heroes are also rightly celebrated as children of the gods, not being themselves begotten of mortal intercourse, but proceeding from their uniform cause, like light concurrent with the essence of a body of light — light, that is, in the open air and pure; after which is conceived the light that is in shadow and becomes mixed with darkness. To this the third, the human, class stands in analogy, by being inclined at times towards vice and forgetfulness, through which man also falls away from always thinking God: he falls short of those who always think him by at times not thinking him, but rises above the irrational creatures by at times thinking him and being recalled to divine knowledge, when he is also ranked in the divine chorus, having escaped material envy and shaken off mortal attachment. Then, therefore, he who has been deemed worthy of divine acceptance is worthy of honour from us too, as one who has adorned a nature equal to ours with a participation in the superior. For it befits the lover of God to honour also whatever has in any way been made like him, whether it possesses that likeness from eternity or happens to have acquired it by practice from some time onward: such are men who have excelled in virtue, concerning whom the present discourse legislates next.
IV · Verse 3
3 and venerate the terrestrial daemons, performing what is lawful.

Human souls adorned with truth and virtue he calls daemons, as being knowing (daēmones) and skilled. Then, distinguishing them from the daemons by nature, who fill the middle class, he called them "terrestrial", as able to live as citizens on earth, to enter earthly bodies and to dwell on the earth; so that by calling them daemons he might separate them from base and ignorant men, as being in a sense unknowing (adaēmones) and not daemons, while by adding "terrestrial" he might set them apart from those who are always knowing and always skilled, and whose nature it is neither to live as citizens on earth nor to share life with earthly bodies. For the title "terrestrial daemon" belongs to none other than one who is a man by nature but has become a daemon by relation; since the third class is properly called earthly, as last among rational beings and turned towards earthly life. For the first was heavenly and the middle aethereal.

Since, then, all men are in this sense terrestrial rational beings, but not all are daemons or wise, he fittingly joined the words together and called wise men "terrestrial daemons". For neither are all men wise, nor are all the wise men; the illustrious heroes and the immortal gods, too, being superior to men by nature, are wise and good. The discourse, then, exhorts us to revere those men who have been ranked with the divine classes, who are equal to daemons and equal to angels and like the illustrious heroes.

For let us not suppose that it bids us honour some base class of daemons, as the word might seem to someone to suggest from common usage. For in general it is not fitting for one who is in love with God and has perceived his own worth to honour what is inferior to human being. Nor shall we honour man himself after the superior beings, unless he has been made like the superior beings and moves with the divine chorus.

What, then, is the honour paid to these? "Performing what is lawful," he says. This is to obey the precepts they have left us, to abide by their words as by laws, and to follow the same road of life which they travelled and did not begrudge sharing with us, but, like some immortal ancestral inheritance, strove to preserve for those who came after them, setting down in writing, for the common benefit, the elements of the virtues and the rules of truth. To obey these and live accordingly is a truer honour to them than if one were to bring them the most costly libations and offer them lavish funeral sacrifices.
Such is the honour of the superior beings, beginning from the Demiurge and ending in good men, by way of the heavenly and aethereal classes in between.

But since we must also take the greatest account of the relations of life, such as fathers and kinsmen (who are not in every case good, but in every case possess, with respect to us, a claim to honour by the worth of the relation), for this reason he adds:
V · Verse 4
4 Honour your parents too, and those most nearly related to you.

Good men, as daemonic and divine, the discourse has laid down that we should revere; but parents, and those who are in some way close to them by natural kinship, whatever they may be like, it bids us honour because of the very necessity of the relation. For what the superior beings are to us according to our eternal kinship — the heavenly beings holding the rank of fathers, the heroes that of honoured kinsmen — this our parents and near relations contribute to us for our mortal life: the near relations being those closest to our parents, and for this reason dignified with the honour that comes after that of parents.

How, then, shall we honour these as well? Is it by directing our own life by their judgement, so as to think and do whatever may be pleasing to them? But in this way the practice of the virtues would be overturned into a zeal for vice, if the fathers should happen to be wicked. Shall we, then, dishonour them in everything because we condemn their vice? And how, then, are we still obeying the present law? And how, if we do not honour the godlike image in our parents or the heroic semblance in our near kin, shall we not commit impiety against those whom we say they resemble? And so the virtue we seem to practise by disobeying our parents will turn into a greater evil — impiety. Yet if we obey our parents in everything, how shall we not in turn fall away from piety and from the rest of virtue, if through depravity of character they should happen not to be guiding us towards what is truly good?

For if what seemed good to the parents were in every case true and good, the honour of parents would be in harmony with the honour of the superior beings. But if the choice of parents is at times deaf to the divine laws, what must those do who have fallen into such a conflict of laws, other than what it is fitting to observe also in the case of other duties that come into opposition through circumstance?

For when greater and lesser goods are set before us, we must prefer the greater to the lesser, whenever it is not possible to preserve both. For example, it is good to obey God, and it is good also to obey one's parents. If, then, obedience to both leads to the same end, the result would be a godsend and free of conflict; but if the divine law carries us one way and our parents another, the choice being at war with itself, we must follow the better, disobeying our parents only in those things in which they themselves do not obey the divine laws. For one who wishes to keep the rules of virtue cannot agree with those who transgress them.

But in all other things we shall honour our parents exceedingly, rendering them the service of our body and the supply of our means as eagerly as possible. For it is just that they should make use of those whom they begot and reared.

But what does not depend on the succession that comes from them, this the law leaves free of their mastery, and bids us seek our true Father, cleave to him, and take the greatest care for our likeness to him. And so it turns out that we can do both — preserve both the divine goods and the human. And we shall neither neglect the care of our parents through a conceit of virtue, nor through senseless compliance admit impiety, the greatest of evils.

For even if they should threaten us with death for disobeying, or with disinheritance, we must not be frightened by such things, but must know well what it is that will suffer them, and that they threaten only what they begot; while that which is beyond suffering these things it befits us to keep free and obedient to God alone.

The true honour of parents, then, which the aim of virtue grants, is that we spare neither our bodies nor our means, but willingly submit ourselves to them in all such things. For it is fitting neither to decline serving our parents with our own hands — rather, the more toilsome and servile that service becomes, the more we should count it an honour — nor to be sparing when our substance is spent, but readily to furnish everything for their need, glad and rejoicing in the labours and expenses undertaken for them. For to do these things gratefully both preserves the law of virtue and repays the debt owed to nature.

Such is the honour of parents. That of near relations, ranked second after it, will measure its service by nearness of nature, allotting to each of our kin as much of the honour that follows that of parents as their nearness to them indicates — it being clear that in their case too virtue remains free of any master.
VI · Verse 5
5 Of all others, make him your friend who is best in virtue.

After the first honour, owed to our kindred above, and the honour that follows it, owed to parents and kinsmen, the law of making friends is handed down in due sequence. It bids us choose the best of those outside our family for friendship and join ourselves to him in the fellowship of the virtues, so that we may have the good man as a friend for a good reason, and may not attach him to ourselves for other uses. Thus this precept resembles the injunction concerning virtuous men who have departed this life. For as there he said that of all men only those who have knowledge ought to be honoured, so here he exhorts us to make friends of the good alone, allowing a choice in the case of others, but in the case of parents and kinsmen being content with nature. For the mere person of a father or a brother brings honour along with it, whereas with others it is virtue that makes a man worthy of honour, just as with those who have departed from life. But the ones ranked before these are worthy of honour by their very nature: there, gods and heroes; here, fathers and kinsmen, who hold out to us, in a mortal nature, images of our immortal kinship. Such, then, is the first pursuit and acquisition of a friend. How he is to be kept, in the way that contributes to our fellowship in good things, and how he is to be set aside, if he is seen to change for the worse and not to heed the counsels that lead to the better — this he says next.
VII · Verses 6–8
6 Yield to gentle words and to helpful deeds, 7 and do not hate your friend for a small fault, 8 so far as you are able; for ability dwells close to necessity.

Here he discusses how we ought to behave towards our friends. And first, that when they propose what is good, and do anything whatever for our benefit, we ought to obey them willingly. For it is to this common good that the law of friendship joins us, so that we may be helped by them towards progress in virtue, and they by us. For as fellow-travellers on the common road of the best life, whatever one of us foresees better than another we must lay down for the common benefit, yielding gently to those friends who guide us well, gently offering them in turn a share in what is good, and never quarrelling with them about money or reputation or any other thing belonging to the mortal order. For that would be to fall into enmity, "for a small fault", with those who are our friends in respect of the greatest goods. In everything, then, we shall bear with our friends, as constrained by the very great necessity of the friendly disposition — except in one thing. We shall not give way to them when they are sliding towards the worse; nor, when they turn from the pursuit of philosophy to some other purpose in life, shall we follow them, being swept along ourselves with those who fall away from the aim of virtue. Rather, if possible, we shall try by every means to set our friend right again; and if we cannot persuade him, we shall keep quiet, neither making him an enemy, because of the friendship that has been, nor any longer a friend, because of his change for the worse. So it is for this reason that we shall at some point set our friend aside: because he can no longer be our partner in virtue, for the sake of which we made him our friend in the first place. But let this setting aside take care not to fall into enmity. For even if he has withdrawn himself from the friendship, we at least must take the greatest pains that he may be called back to what is right: not being glad at our friend's fall, nor looking down on the weakness of his judgment, but rather grieving and lamenting, feeling deep pain for him and praying for him, and trying to do everything that may lead him back to salvation through repentance. Such things are these: not to quarrel with him over money or reputation, not to deprive him of our fellowship by way of insult, and not to make his misfortune a matter of pride for ourselves.

Now since our forbearance contributes most of all to the best keeping of friends, to their reasonable setting aside and to their recall through repentance — our not haggling with friends over anything, not taking things with them in the utmost rigour, but being as patient as possible — for this reason he added "so far as you are able". Then, so that no one should measure ability by the standard of his own choice, but by what nature itself can bear, as much as necessity discovers when it comes upon us, he added "for ability dwells close to necessity". For each person is proved by necessity to be able to do more than he thinks he can. We must therefore be willing to bear with our friends as far as necessity shows that we are able, and to make bearable, through the necessity of friendship, even what at first appeared unbearable. For let us not suppose that only what is imposed on us by force should be nobly endured; we must also count the things that tend to the keeping and recall of friends as worthy of still greater endurance, as injunctions of divine necessity. And with men of good sense the necessity of the intellect is more powerful than force from without. Whether, then, you look to the necessity that arises from circumstance, or to the voluntary necessity — that which is made up of the rules of knowledge and descends from the divine laws — you will discover the measure of ability that is in you. This measure the discourse now tells us we must bring to bear upon our friends, when it commands us not to be hastily set at enmity with them "for a small fault". It counts all things outside the soul as small, and forbids us, from a grudging attachment to these things, to make our friend an enemy; rather, through indifference to such things, we should call back even the friend who has fallen away, and in every case be conscious within ourselves that, so far as lay in us, we both kept the friends we had and won back those who had slid towards the worse, and that we neither began any enmity nor repaid in kind one who had become an enemy of his own accord.

For this is what the ordinance of friendship prescribes, since friendship is the greatest virtue and appears upon the others as their perfection. For the end of the virtues is friendship, and their beginning is piety. The principle of piety is in us the seed of all good things, while the state of friendship is the most perfect fruit of the virtues. As, then, we must observe justice not only towards those who deal justly with us but also towards those who attempt to wrong us, lest by wronging them in return we fall into the same evil condition as they, so we must also hold fast to friendship — that is, to love of mankind towards all who share our kind. But we shall set the measures of friendship in their fitting order: the good we shall embrace in every way, both for their nature and for their disposition, as preserving the perfection of man; the bad we shall love for the sake of our common nature alone, since they offer us nothing from their disposition towards the choice of friendship. Hence it is rightly said that no one is an enemy to the virtuous man, and that only the good man is a friend to the good. For as one who loves man as man, he holds not even the bad man to be an enemy; but as one who seeks a man adorned with virtue for fellowship, he chooses the good out of all, imitating God even in the measures of friendship — God, who hates no human being, but embraces the good man above all. For, holding out the good of his love for mankind to the whole race in common, he grants to each his fitting portion, leading the good up to himself, and directing the fugitives from virtue towards what is right by the laws of Justice. For this is both proportionate and beneficial to each. So it befits us also to keep friendship towards all men, with the distribution according to worth.

For we shall also have temperance and justice towards all, and not towards the just and temperate alone; nor shall we be good to the good and bad to the bad. For if we changed so readily along with whoever we happened upon, we should have no good of our own that we kept always and towards all. But if we have acquired virtue as a settled state, it is not in the power of whoever wishes to draw us away from it; nor shall we alter our dispositions to match those we meet, being fortunate in the permanence of virtue. What holds, then, for the other virtues must be kept in the case of friendship too, since friendship, as we said, is the greatest virtue, and love of mankind is seen in common towards all but in a special way towards the good; which is why the name "love of mankind" is the more fitting for it. So much for these things; let us go on to what follows.
VIII · Verses 9–11
9 Know these things so; and accustom yourself to master these: 10 the belly first of all, and sleep, and lust, 11 and anger.

All these must be restrained and set in order, so that they may not disturb our reasoning. Come, then, let us bridle the whole irrational part and bring it into order by right training, since its parts in succession furnish vice to one another. Thus the belly, when overfilled, brings on much sleep; both together produce an abundance of seed, which rouses immoderately to sexual pleasure and whets the appetitive part of the soul towards licentiousness. And the spirited part, swept along with this, rushes into every kind of fight: now avenging wrongs over food and drink, now fighting over courtesans, and at other times contending to acquire one pleasure or another. "Accustom yourself", then, "to master these", beginning from the belly first, so that the irrational forms of the soul may become obedient to reason, and that you yourself, by your own efforts, may be able to keep undeviatingly piety, honour towards parents and all that the discourse enjoined a little earlier. For these precepts that follow are the power by which the former are kept, since all of those would be transgressed if the passionate powers did not follow reason. For either anger has stirred a man up against his parents, or desire has armed him to disobey them; and again, either anger has roused him to blasphemy, or desire of money to perjury. In general, evil deeds are done through these powers, when the rational soul does not direct them to what is right. Hence come impieties of every kind, wars among kinsmen, betrayals of friends and every form of lawlessness, so that some are even compelled to cry out:I know what evils I am about to do, but anger is stronger than my counsels,
and others, or the same people at another time, to cry:
I know what evils I am about to do, but desire is stronger than my counsels,
and:
You seem to me to speak well, but I feel what most people feel: I am not entirely persuaded by you.

For the rational class, being naturally well disposed to the perception of what is noble, is easily brought to recollection and easily led to the teaching of right reason, provided it is not dragged down towards vice by the pulls of passion, as by so many weights of lead. We must therefore both know for ourselves what we ought to do, and accustom the irrational powers, as far as possible, to follow the reason within us as well. For when the passions have been set in order in this way, our reasoning would be able to keep without distraction the first precepts, about which it was said, "Know these things so". But about those that follow he said, "accustom yourself to master", showing that the rational part is ordered by teaching and knowledge, the irrational by habituation and a kind of bodily moulding; just as irrational animals, too, are led by men through habit alone. The belly, then, once accustomed to seek what is moderate, renders the other desires of the body more orderly and the spirit more harmonious, so that we may deliberate in quiet about what we ought to do, without being greatly troubled by the passions that beset us. From this we are also taught to know ourselves, what we are in truth, and to respect ourselves once we have attained that knowledge. And from this knowledge, and from the reverence that accompanies it, comes the avoidance of shameful things. For evils are called shameful as being unfitting and unworthy to be done by a rational being. Concerning these he goes on to say:
IX · Verses 11–12
11 Never do anything shameful, either with another 12 or by yourself; and above all, feel shame before yourself.

For either, when acting on our own, we regard some shameful deed as indifferent, which we would never have done with another, out of shame before our partner in the act; or conversely, in going along with certain people, we do what we would never have done on our own, drawn into boldness in the deed by the fellowship of those who act with us. For this reason he has cut off in advance both roads of deviation into what is shameful and evil. For if the shameful is truly to be shunned, it could never become worthy of choice because of circumstance. Therefore he joined the two and said, "either with another or by yourself", so that neither solitude may rouse you to what is unfitting nor company make your fault easy to excuse. Then he added the reason, the only one that turns us away from evils: "and above all, feel shame before yourself". For if you accustom yourself to feel shame before yourself, you will have everywhere one before whom you will feel shame, a guardian most intimately your own and impossible to escape. For many, when left alone by friends or servants, have done the very things they were ashamed to do before because of them. Had they, then, no one with them? I leave God aside, for he is too far removed from the awareness of the wicked; but did they not have themselves, and the tribunal of conscience? They had indeed; but they did not know that they had it, being overpowered by their passions. Such people held the rational part within them in no honour, and treated it as viler than a slave. Take yourself, then, as the guardian most intimately your own, and, turning back towards him, begin the turning away from evils. For each man's shame before himself necessarily becomes the avoidance of things shameful and unworthy of the rational being. How he who thus disdains evils is brought into kinship with virtue, he tells us next.
X · Verses 13–16

13 Next, practise justice in deed and in word, 14 and do not accustom yourself to act thoughtlessly in anything; 15 but know that death is appointed for all, 16 and that wealth is wont now to be gained, now to be lost.

He who feels shame before himself becomes his own guard against ever falling into vice. But vice has several forms. In the rational part it is folly; in the spirited part, cowardice; in the appetitive part, love of pleasure and love of money; and in all the powers together, injustice. So we needed a tetrad of virtues to turn away such evils: practical wisdom for the reasoning part, courage for the spirited part, temperance for the appetitive part, and justice for all the powers together — justice being the most perfect of all the virtues and containing the others as its own parts. That is why the discourse mentioned it first; then practical wisdom, and after it the best practices that are born of practical wisdom and contribute to the completeness of justice. For he who uses right reasoning acquires courage as his ally in dangers, temperance in pleasures, and justice in all things together. And thus practical wisdom is found to be the beginning of the virtues, justice their end, and courage and temperance in between. For the power that reasons out all things and always seeks what is suitable to each in our actions, so that each may be disposed reasonably, is the state of practical wisdom. It is the best disposition of our rational being, and from it good order comes to the other powers too, so that the spirit is courageous, desire temperate, and justice holds to proportion; and in this way our mortal man is adorned from the abundance of the virtue that is in the immortal man. For the virtues shine primarily from the intellect into the rational soul, and they are its proper form, its perfection and its well-being; while into the irrational part and the mortal body there comes a certain participation in the virtues, so that what has grown together with the rational being may also be filled with seemliness and measure.

This practical wisdom, the leader of the divine goods, when it has been well established in the rational soul, enables us to deliberate well about everything, to bear death courageously and the loss of wealth gently and with composure. For practical wisdom is able to endure all the vicissitudes of mortal nature, and of the fortune that follows it, with temperance and without dismay. For it has reckoned out the nature of things, and knows that what was compounded of earth and water must of necessity be dissolved into them again; and it does not rage against necessity, nor does it hold that our affairs are without providence if what is mortal dies. For it knows "that death is appointed for all", and that there is a fixed time for the continuance of our mortal bodies; and when this arrives we must not be aggrieved, but follow willingly, as a divine law. For this is what "appointed" signifies here: that our mortal life is bounded by certain necessary limits; and that it is proper to practical wisdom to follow the decrees of the superior beings, since practical wisdom seeks not to avoid dying but to die well. Likewise it is not ignorant of the nature of wealth either: that now it has come and now it has gone, according to certain definite causes, which it is foolish to resist. For we are not masters of the acquisition of things that are not in our power. Not in our power are the body and wealth, and, in a word, whatever lies outside our rational being: neither to acquire them in the first place is in our power, nor to keep them as long as we wish. But to receive them when they come and to part with them when they go, and to do so with virtue — this is in our power and proper to the rational being, if it does not accustom itself to behave thoughtlessly about what happens, but follows the divine measures by which all that concerns us is defined. Here, then, what is in our power has its greatest force: in judging well about what is not in our power, and not, through an inordinate attachment to these things, losing the virtue of self-determination as well. What, then, does sensible judgment say? To use the body and wealth well while they are present, and for the service of virtue; and when they depart, to know what is right, and to gain, besides the other virtues, freedom from grief. For in this way piety towards the gods will be kept, and the measures of justice, if the rational part learns to use circumstances well and nobly, and to set the rules of practical wisdom against the things that seem to happen by chance and without order. For otherwise virtue could not be kept, unless a certain right belief is present in the rational being. For it cannot follow the superior beings as superior, but will be disposed like one coerced by tyrants; nor will it take any account of those who live with it, nor discover the best management of body or of wealth, once it has accustomed itself to behave thoughtlessly. For see how those who flee death at any cost, or long to keep their money, will necessarily resort to many acts of injustice and blasphemy: when they fall into what they senselessly fled, they utter unholy curses against the gods and declare that they exercise no providence; and they wrong others unsparingly, and try to amass everyone's goods for what they think is their own advantage. And so the harm done by false belief becomes manifest in them, in that the greatest of evils spring up: injustice towards their equals and impiety towards the superior beings. From these he would be pure who obeys the verses before us: he who by well-reasoned judgment nobly endures death, and does not think the loss of wealth unbearable. From these he also takes his starting points towards justice: that one must abstain from what belongs to others, harm no one, and not make the misfortunes of others one's own profit. But none of these things will be kept by the man who supposes that his own soul is mortal and has accustomed himself to behave thoughtlessly, never reckoning what it is in us that dies and has need of wealth, and what it is that practises virtue and is benefited by it. For only the distinction between these could supply eagerness for the practice of virtue, and the inspired impulse that comes from "Know yourself" and "Feel shame before yourself" could rouse us to the acquisition of what is noble. For it is by our own worth that we must measure our duties towards others as well, in deeds and in words. And the unswerving keeping of our duties would be justice; that is why it is set before the other virtues, to become the measure of duties. For "practise justice", he says, "in deed and in word". You will not, then, speak any blasphemy when you lose your wealth or suffer the pains of disease, so that you may not be unjust in word; nor will you seize what belongs to your neighbours or contrive misfortunes for men, so that you may not be unjust in deed. For while justice garrisons the soul, we shall do what is fitting both towards men and towards ourselves.

But the best measure of justice is practical wisdom. Hence to "practise justice" he added "and do not accustom yourself to act thoughtlessly in anything", since justice cannot subsist without practical wisdom. For that is truly just which perfect practical wisdom defines. And this would be the practical wisdom that is thoughtless about nothing, but is circumspect about the body and circumspect also about what contributes to its needs; that counts all things less precious than virtue, and holds as the greatest benefit the best disposition of the rational soul, by which everything else too is adorned according to its capacity. Such, then, is the aim of the verses before us: to set forth the tetrad of the practical virtues and hand it down to the hearers, together with the wakeful watchfulness and vigilance that befits words and deeds. For one part of them delivers practical wisdom, another courage, another temperance; the part placed before them urges the practice of justice, which is observed in common over all the other virtues; and the words "wealth is wont now to be gained, now to be lost" show that liberality, too, accompanies the temperate disposition, liberality being a virtue concerned with the income and expenditure of money. For to acquire it and to part with it only when reason allows removes in advance the occasions of meanness and of prodigality.

All these things proceed, as from a source and first principle, from feeling shame before oneself. And this precept already embraces within itself "Know yourself", which must underlie all earnest actions and all contemplative knowledge. For otherwise how shall we know that it befits us to moderate our passions and to know the things that are? For doubts are raised about these: first, whether they are possible for men; then, whether they are beneficial to those who possess them. For, quite the contrary, the virtuous man seems to come off worse in the affairs of life, because he does not take unjustly from where he should not, and spends justly on what he should; and as to the body he lies more open to attack than anyone, since he neither seeks office himself nor servilely courts those in office. So that, if there were not some other being in us that is benefited by virtue, we would hardly give up wealth or power for its sake. Hence those who think the soul mortal are being clever rather than truthful when they speak of not abandoning virtue. For if there were not something of us that remains after death, and this of a nature to be adorned with truth and virtue — such as we say the rational soul is — there could be no pure longing in us for what is noble. For the suspicion of perishing stifles in advance all earnestness about these things, and leads us to bodily enjoyments, of whatever kind they may be and from wherever they can be procured. For how, on their view, will it seem the part of a sensible or moderately composed man not to gratify the body in everything, since it is through the body that even the existence of the soul is preserved — the soul not existing by itself, but supervening upon a certain configuration of the body? And how shall we give up the body for the sake of virtue, when we are about to destroy the soul itself together with the body, so that the virtue, for love of which we endured death, is nowhere? But concerning these matters it has been sufficiently demonstrated by divine men both that the soul is immortal and that it is by nature adorned by virtue alone.

Now, having set our seal on the present doctrine, let us pass on to what follows, adding only this much to what has been said: that just as all vice flows in through ignorance of our own being, so through knowledge of ourselves, and disdain for what does not befit the rational nature, the unerring keeping of our duties is found in every case; and this becomes the measure of the particular virtues. For by looking to our own being as to a rule, we find what is due in all things, living according to right reason in harmony with our own being. For everything that makes the soul better and leads it up to the well-being that befits its nature is truly virtue and the law of philosophy; but what aims only at human decorum is servile sophistry and a shadow-painting of what is noble, hunting the praise of the many and taking all its care to seem good, not to be good. So much for these things.

It follows of necessity from right reasoning that we should not behave thoughtlessly about the things that seem to happen in life without order either, but should have well and nobly reasoned out their causes, and bear them without complaining of the beings who have the care of us. For they, distributing to each what is fitting according to worth, have not judged all those who did not live alike in their former lives worthy of equal things. For if there is providence, and our soul is incorruptible in essence but moves towards virtue or vice by a self-moved choice, how could the guardians of the law that requires each to be treated according to his deserts render equal things to those who are unequal, and not assign to each the fitting fortune, which man is said to receive by lot when he comes forth into generation? If, then, it is no myth that there is a providence which assigns to each what befits him, and that our soul is immortal, it is clear that we must transfer the cause of our sufferings from the one who governs all to ourselves; and from this, reason will grant us the power to heal our hardships as well. For when we have found in ourselves the causes of so great an inequality, first, by the rightness of our judgment we shall lighten the burden of what befalls us; then, by the sacred methods and by right admonitions retuning the soul to what is better, we shall set ourselves wholly free from what is painful. But when a man suffers ill, not even to perceive the causes, nor to divine what is fittingly befalling him, is the mark of one who has accustomed himself to behave thoughtlessly about everything — which the discourse has now forbidden. For whoever has not sought out the true cause must transfer the charge to the superior being: either that it does not exist at all, or that it does not care for us rightly. And such opinions not only intensify the evils that come from a former life, but also rouse the soul to every kind of wickedness, and deprive it of its self-determined healing, by adding hidden causes to the troubles it now endures. How one ought to philosophise about these matters, hear from the verses themselves.
XI · Verses 17–20

17 Of all the pains that mortals suffer by divine fortunes, 18 whatever lot you have, bear it gently and do not chafe at it. 19 Yet it is fitting to heal it as far as you can; and consider this: 20 the lot does not give very much of these to the good.

Before we go further in the explanation, this must first be said: that by "pains" he here means the things that are laborious and that make the road of life rougher for us — such as disease, poverty, the loss of those dearest to us, and want of honour in one's city. For these are indeed hard, and difficult to manage in the course of life; yet they are not truly evils, nor are they harmful to the soul itself, unless the soul itself chooses to decline into vice on account of one of them — which it might suffer equally in the case of things that seem good, if it is not willing to make a good use of them, such as health, wealth and power. For it is possible to become bad even in these, and to acquire virtue in their opposites. But the things that are truly evil are the faults committed by choice, with which virtue by its nature cannot enter in together. These are injustice, licentiousness, and everything that does not admit of being yoked with the noble. For with none of these can one join the word "nobly": one does not say, "he is unjust nobly," "he is licentious nobly," as we say of external evils, "he is ill nobly," "he is poor nobly," when a man bears such things well and in accordance with right reason. To the vices of the soul the word "nobly" is not applied, because they are turnings-away from right reason and failures of it — the reason which is present in the human soul by nature and inscribed in it, but which the soul overlooks, blinded by passionate attachment.

A proof that right reason is present in men is this: that even the unjust man, in matters where nothing is at stake for him, judges justly, and the licentious man temperately; and, in a word, the bad man makes use of right apprehensions wherever he is free from passionate attachment. This is why the base man is able to change over to virtue by condemning his former vice. Yet it does not follow that there must also be present in us a reason which is not right, to be the principle of the vices as the other is of the virtues. For right reason, by its presence, is sufficient — like the law in a city — to distinguish what is done in accordance with it from what is done against it, and to approve the one and correct the other. And there is no need of a principle of evils, whether one that lies within us or one that implants an evil-working cause from without; but there is need, above all and alone, of a principle of goods: both of one separate from rational beings, such as God is, and of one present within them and governing them by an essential contact, such as right reason is.

Such, then, is the distinction among evils. Of these, he says that it is not those which depend on choice that are allotted to men by divine fortune, but those which depend on circumstance — things which now lie among what is not in our power, but which long ago followed upon faults of choice: painful, as we said, yet capable of receiving the ornament that comes from virtue. For a temperate way of life has adorned poverty; practical wisdom has redeemed a mean extraction; and the just life has borne the loss of children gently — the life that can say, "My child is dead? Then he has been given back," and, "I knew that I had begotten a mortal." And in the same way all other things too, when clothed with the beauty of virtue, become more seemly.

Next the discourse inquires what these divine fortunes are, according to which mortals meet with outward hardships. For if the divine judgment, of its primary intent, gives wealth to this man and poverty to another, this ought to be called a divine choice, and not fortune. And if nothing presides over the allotment of such things, but it falls out at random and of itself that one man is fortunate, as they say, and another unfortunate, this ought to be called fortune, and not divine fortune. But if the God who governs us apportions to each what is fitting according to his desert, and is not the cause of our being of this kind or of that, but is sole master of rendering requital according to the ordinances of justice, then with good reason did he join the two words and call the sentences of the judgment "divine fortunes": insofar as that which judges is divine and intellective, he called them "divine" (daimoniai), that is, knowing; and insofar as that which is judged becomes bad by its own choice, and so becomes deserving of these hardships, he added the word "fortunes" — because it is not God's purpose, of his primary intent, to punish or to honour this or that particular person, but always the one who has become of such or such a kind; and the cause of this lies in us. The interweaving, then, of our choice with his judgment produces fortune, so that the whole of this — the divine sentence upon our faults — is "divine fortune." And thus the skilful invention of the names brings in together both the divine superintendence and the soul's self-determination and immortality; and it shows that neither do all things come about by fate or by providence, nor at random and by chance, nor is all our life disposed by our own unaided choice. Rather, whatever faults we commit among the things in our power are to be referred to choice; whatever follows upon those faults according to the laws of justice, to fate; the goods bestowed by God of his primary intent, to providence; while to the random and the chance we must refer the cause of nothing that is, nor even of anything that comes to be — except that, by accident, through the interweaving of what is brought about primarily by providence, fate and choice, the element of chance will follow upon the first-working causes.

Take an example. The judge wishes to punish the murderer, and not this particular man; yet he punishes this man too, whom he did not wish to punish, when the man has himself put himself into the rank of murderer. And the judge's sentence against the murderer is primary, while the sentence against this particular man is accidental, because he willingly assumed the character of the murderer. And again, the wicked man wished to murder, but was unwilling to pay the penalty for it. So that in his case too the murderous disposition is primary, as depending on the soul's self-determination, while the rackings and tortures that follow upon it follow by accident. And the cause of all these is the law, which both implants in the judge the choice to punish the wicked and brings upon the murderer the sentence of punishment. Reckon, I pray you, this same thing in the case of the divine superintendence too: when a human choice has willed to do evil, and the choice of judges who guard the law strives by every means to correct evils, their concurrence produces divine fortune, according to which he who has wrought such deeds becomes deserving of such punishments. The choosing of what is base refers its cause to the self-determination of the one judged; the punishment that follows according to desert, to the law-guarding knowledge of the judges; and what brings the two together is the law, which ordained that all things should be good so far as possible, and nothing base. For this law, pre-existing in the goodness of God, does not allow the wicked to go unaccountable, lest evil, remaining in them, drive them into complete insensibility to the good — of which the justice administered by the guardians of the law supplies the necessary reminder.

The law, then, as has been said, brings together those whose nature is to judge and those whose nature is to become bad, working out through both its own proper good. For if paying the penalty is more profitable than not paying it, and justice looks to the correction of the excess of evils, it is plain that the law has joined these two kinds together for benefiting and being benefited: setting the judging kind, as guardian of the law, over the other, and handing over the kind whose nature is to err and be judged, as transgressor of the law, to the better kind, to be dealt with according to its desert, so that it may at some time come to recollection and awareness of the law through which it suffers ill. For the law which men deny in doing ill, they long for in suffering ill. For example, the man who does wrong wishes that there were no God, so that he may not have the penalty hanging over him like the stone of Tantalus; but the man who is wronged wishes that there be a God, so that he may obtain help for what he has suffered. That is why those who do wrong must be brought round in their turn to being wronged, so that what they did not see in doing, drunk with the passion of greed, they may learn in suffering, schooled by the pain of loss — if, that is, they undergo their penalty well. But if through the recklessness of their choice they still grow worse, they themselves are perhaps less benefited; yet they certainly become an instructive example to those who are right-minded and able to perceive the causes of such sufferings.

Let us accept these as the most sovereign principles of the judgment: the goodness of God; the law that proceeds from it; and the right reason within us, which is transgressed and offended against as though it were an indwelling god. And the outcome of the judgment is these "pains," as he calls them — all that makes our life rougher through injuries to the body and to outward things. These the present discourse bids us bear gently, taking to heart their causes, cutting them down as far as possible, and turning to our benefit what seems harmful — above all by making ourselves worthy of the divine goods through the highest virtue. But if anyone does not yet aspire to this, let him at least attain the civic goods through the middle virtue. For this was what we are enjoined to do, in order to suffer painful things well and to heal them. What, then, is the cure, if not all that has been said above, from which both the reasonable endurance of pains and the method of treating them are shown?

The sum of what has been said is this: God, being at once lawgiver and judge, establishes goods and abolishes evils; and therefore he is in no way the cause of evils. But those who have become bad by self-determined impulses, and have forgotten the right reason within them, he punishes — as bad, by the law that forbids evils; and as men, by the supervening interweaving of the law with their choice, which we call fortune. For the law does not punish a man simply as man, but as bad. And of his becoming bad his choice held the first cause; but once he has become bad (which was in our power and not in God's), then he pays the penalty (which was in the power of the divine law and not in ours). And the only aim of the law that could be both befitting God and beneficial to us is to cut short vice, to purge it away by the manifold corrections of justice, and to turn the soul that has fallen under wickedness back to the recollection of right reason. And so, while the law stands fast and always pronounces the same things, each man, making his desert now one thing and now another, does not always meet with the same things; for that would be neither just nor to our advantage. It is the change in the one judged that brings about the change in the judgment: for how can one who has not remained the same be deemed worthy of the same things?

One must, therefore, bear the divine fortunes well, and not chafe while paying the penalty, but be purified — so far as the divine judgment is concerned — through the very things that seem to be hindrances to the comfort of life here. And such reasoning becomes both a healing of past faults and a turning back to the right reason that is within us. For how shall the man who holds painful things to be the fruits of vice not flee the cause that brings him down into them? And if one must be angry amid what is grievous, will he not think he ought to be angry with himself rather than with God, who checks wickedness through the instruments of justice — instruments through which we may understand and recollect how good a thing it was, after all, not to stand apart from the divine laws, nor to become bad of our own will? For painful things are not distributed to men at random, if indeed God and the bounds of justice preside over us, bringing upon each the lot he deserves. Therefore it is reasonable too that painful things do not befall the good very much.

For, first, they will bear them gently, through their contentment with the divine judgment and through the acquisition of virtue, by which hard things become gentler. And their life is full of good hope that for the future such things will in no way trouble us, since, if we have become good, the divine goods are laid up for us according to the highest virtue, and the human goods according to the middle state. Then, too, they will heal such things as far as they can, from the very fact of bearing them gently, being taught the methods of their treatment. For how is it possible to make use of sacred supplications in a manner befitting the gods, unless we hold that providence and justice watch over human affairs, and that our soul, being immortal, meets on each occasion with such outward things as it has made itself worthy of by the movements of its choice? For the man who does not refer his present lot to these causes — whence will he take the starting-points for bearing it gently? Whence the art of healing it? It is impossible to say. For one cannot be content with such things directly, as though they were indifferent, or even better than their opposites, since in themselves they appear to be things to be avoided, being painful and laborious. And our nature does not embrace such things as desirable for their own sake, unless some good is expected in return for the patient endurance of hardships.
