It follows of necessity, then, that one is vexed, is filled with discontent, and aggravates one's pains still further out of ignorance about our own essence — and pays the penalty none the less; and, worse, that we acquire the greatest vice, if we think the universe to be without providence or badly cared for. And this is the same as thinking that God does not exist, or that, existing, he exercises no providence, or that, exercising providence, he is not good and just — opinions which hold together every kind of impiety and which drive the man who is possessed by such notions into every vice. For as piety has shown itself to be the mother of the virtues, so the falling away from piety is the leader of all vice.

He alone, then, will find the cure of these things who has been thoroughly taught to bear them gently. And this comes through philosophy alone, which knows exactly the essences of all beings and the activities that follow upon their essences, whose sequence and ordered arrangement is the governance of the universe — from which, too, the divine fortunes are necessarily apportioned; and the desert apportioned to each, which is here called "lot" (moira), depends on the providence of God, on the good order of the cosmos, and on human choice. For if there were no providence of God, there would be no order in the cosmos — which one might also call fate. And if these did not exist, there would be no justice and judgment of the wicked, nor any honour and approval of the good. But since providence and order exist, all who are now born ought to meet with equal goods, if they had contributed nothing of their own towards the inequality. Yet they plainly do not meet with equal things. It is clear, then, that the inequality of choice, submitted to the judgment of providence, does not permit an equal lot to be apportioned to them, if indeed they must meet with what accords with their desert.

Nor let it trouble us that the same unevenness appears in irrational animals, in plants, and even in inanimate things, as among men. For it does not follow that our affairs are unprovided for because these things befall those beings at random; nor that there are among them too justice and judgment and reckonings of virtue and vice because our affairs are so exactly regulated. For, first, inanimate things are set out as common matter for plants, animals and men; next, plants are set before animals and men as common food, and some animals too before animals and men. Hence these act upon one another without considering the desert of those that suffer, but relieving their own hunger or sickness, and in general filling up their own want from wherever they can. So that our need, filled from whatever lies at hand, is the occasion of misfortune for animals, and our fondness for them is the cause of their seeming good fortune. Now if the argument, as it went on, had introduced in turn some other beings superior to us, who made use of us to fill up their own want as we are seen to use irrational creatures, we should have to admit that those beings were mortal, and human bodies would be seen to be consumed for their need. But if nothing of what stands above man is mortal (since man himself is the last of the rational kinds, and for this reason, though immortal, comes into a mortal body through a change of condition, and, taking up an instrument akin to the irrational creatures, lives his life upon earth), then there can be nothing that would use our misfortunes for its own feast; and therefore nothing that would make disorderly use of us in its eagerness to be filled. Justice and order, then, lay down for the immortals who stand above us the bounds of their governance concerning us: to contrive for us those things which lessen our vice here and are able to turn us back towards them. For they care for us as for kinsmen who have fallen. Hence Reverence and Nemesis and Shame, which turn us away from evils, are rightly said to have regard for men alone; for the rational animal alone is by nature capable of perceiving justice.

It is fitting, then, that we, who are separated from the irrational creatures by the widest bounds, should also be under a governance that differs very greatly from theirs. For the ordinance of providence too is proportioned to the essences of beings; and as each thing was brought into existence by the Demiurgic God, so is it also deemed worthy of providence. And it appears that, in the case of human souls, he brought each one into existence himself, but in the case of irrational creatures only the kinds, handing them over to the nature that moulds them — as is the view of Plato and of Timaeus the Pythagorean, who hold that nothing mortal is an immediate work of God, but that human souls come to be from the same mixing-bowl as the encosmic gods and the daemons, that is, the illustrious heroes. Therefore providence extends to men individually, one by one: how each departs from the things there; how he inclines towards the things here; how he lives here; how he may be brought back from here to there. None of this need be considered in regard to irrational life. For it did not descend hither through being unable to follow a god; nor can it sojourn on earth as a heavenly plant; nor is it of a nature to be led back up to some consort star.

Let this, for the present, serve as our defence against the malcontents who, from every quarter, build up the case for a world without providence. To them it is right to say this too: that from bearing hardships gently the human way of life shows itself reasonable, both lightening hardships for the present and healing them for the future. But you, by chafing, what good will you do — unless it be only to add to your toils the greatest of evils, impiety, and to make the hardships themselves rougher for yourselves by thinking that you suffer them beyond your desert? For the sick man who frets at being sick will, for that very reason, be the sicker. Therefore one must not be angry when requital is made according to desert, lest through blasphemous discontent at our present lot we come into a still worse condition. Let us look at it this way too. If someone who has fallen into poverty bears it gently, then besides the freedom from grief that gentleness brings, he will also find some consolation for his life: on the one hand, because his reasoning, not being confounded by grief, finds means of a reasonable livelihood; on the other, because his neighbours, admiring his sensible endurance, help as far as they can to provide him with the necessities of life. But the man who chafes and grows bitter like a woman first brings upon himself voluntary griefs besides; then, bound fast to lamenting his poverty, he becomes utterly without resource, neither having the leisure to contribute anything himself towards a livelihood, nor receiving any contribution from his neighbours, except what someone may toss him out of pity — which in turn, through the disposition of the giver, only increases the grief of the man reduced to such need.

From all that has been said, then, one must bear what befalls gently, and heal it as far as one can, reckoning out its causes by undistorted notions, and seeing that, since providence exists, the man who has now become good is not neglected, even though he drags after him the brands of ancient wrath. For by the very acquiring of virtue he escapes their painfulness and finds their cure, bringing from himself the help of freedom from grief, and receiving from providence release from hardships. For our own vice, and the divine judgment that punishes wickedness, heaped up these hardships; and with reason they are dissolved again both by our own virtue and by the law of providence, which releases from evils those who by their own efforts have advanced towards the good.

So much we may take from these verses too, in the way of doctrines that contribute to the elements of virtue. For they have been shown to contain the truest accounts of providence, of fate, and of what is in our power, by which the discourse has set straight the difficulty raised by the unevenness of appearances, and has shown throughout that God is not the cause of any evil. And if one joins these to what went before, a single argument will emerge from them all, confirming the everlastingness of the soul. For the practice of justice, dying nobly, and a liberal disposition towards wealth require most of all, for their establishment, that the soul does not die together with the body, as has already been said. And the bearing of divine fortunes gently, and the being able to heal them, has now been shown to require that the soul is not born together with the body. From both it is demonstrated that the soul is superior to generation and corruption, and is an essence other than the mortal body, being in and by itself everlasting. For it is not possible that something which has come forth into generation from some point in time should endure for ever, just as it is not possible that what has its existence from everlasting should ever admit of corruption. If, then, the human soul, enduring after the corruption of the body, meets with justice and judgment, and receives the requitals due to its desert for what it practised in life, and if it is not possible for what has come to be from a point in time to endure for ever, it is clear that it existed before this too, through all time. And thus the human soul too is found to be among the everlasting offspring of the Demiurgic God; and from this it has its share in likeness to God. But since this too has received a moderate reminder, it is time to consider what follows.
XII · Verses 21–24
21 Many words, both base and noble, fall upon men's ears; 22 be not dismayed by them, nor yet let yourself 23 be kept from them. But if some falsehood is spoken, 24 yield gently.

Human choice, since it is fixed neither always in virtue nor always in vice, has also given birth to the words that go forth through the voice as inclining both ways, since they resemble its own contrary dispositions. Hence some words have come to be true and others false, some good and others bad. This difference requires a discernment grounded in knowledge, so that we may choose the better and reject the worse, and may neither fall sick of an utter misology because we condemn the worse words, nor admit all words without distinction because we accept the better. For misology brings with it that we deprive ourselves even of good words, and an undiscerning love of words that we are harmed, without noticing it, by words that have been corrupted. Let us therefore practise the love of words, but together with the best judgment, so that the love of hearing may draw in every kind of word, while judgment thrusts away the worse. And in this way we shall keep the Pythagorean precept, neither being overawed by the wicked among words and admitting them without examination for this very reason, that they are words; nor being kept away from the good, because they were words just like the worse. For, in the first place, the one kind should not be pursued in so far as they are words, but in so far as they are true; nor should the other be condemned as words, but as false. And, in the second place, we may boldly assert this too: that only true words are words (logoi). For they alone preserve the dignity of rational being, and are the offspring of a soul that is stretched up towards the best and possesses its own proper order; whereas false words are not truly words at all, for, since they carry one towards vice and false opinion, they have renounced the nobility of words, and are the utterances of a soul bereft of reason and defiled with passions.

Receive them not all, then, he says, lest you receive the false as well; nor reject them all, lest you reject the true as well. For either course is absurd: to hate the good together with the worse, or to admit the false for the sake of the better. We ought, then, to praise the good, and, having received them, to exercise ourselves in them, and to examine in what way and how far they lay hold of the truth; and against the false we must acquire the power to contend — the power, namely, which the science of logic supplies for discerning truth from falsehood. And when we are able to overthrow falsehoods, we ought to do it neither with vehemence nor insultingly, but to pursue the truth with gentleness and to refute falsehood with kindly arguments, and, as the verse itself says, "if some falsehood is spoken," to "yield gently" — not granting that the matter is as it is said to be, but hearing it without anger. For by "yield gently" he does not mean that we should give our assent to the falsehood, but that we should hear it with patience, and not be dismayed if some, being men, have fallen away from the truth to their own harm. For the nature of man is fruitful in many perverse opinions, whenever it does not rightly follow the common notions. It is no wonder, then, says the argument, if a man who has neither learned nor discovered anything of the truth has come to such a pitch of folly as to adopt opinions contrary to the truth. On the contrary, it would be a wonder if someone who is willing neither to learn nor to seek should stumble upon the truth of his own accord, as if some god had appeared to him, as in a tragedy. We must therefore hear with indulgence those who speak falsely, and learn by experience from what evils we ourselves have been purified: through the fellowship of a kindred nature we are subject to the same passions, but through the evil-averting power of knowledge we have come to stand on the opposite side of them. And the confidence that knowledge inspires also contributes greatly to gentleness; for a soul that is sufficiently prepared to overcome the deviations from truth will bear false opinions without disturbance, having reckoned out beforehand, in its very apprehension of the truth, everything that departs from the truth. What, then, will disturb such a man as though it were insoluble? What will give him an impression of strength, when he has already overcome every falsehood in advance? It is not, then, from moral virtue alone that the man of knowledge will have his freedom from disturbance, but also from his confidence in contests of this kind.
So much for the discernment of words that is grounded in knowledge. As to the state, proof against deception in all things, which the man of knowledge ought to possess, he immediately adds:
XIII · Verses 24–26
24 And what I tell you now, let it be fulfilled in every case: 25 let no one by word or deed induce you 26 to do or say what is not best for you.
This precept extends to all things, and is equivalent to what was said somewhere above:
11 Never do anything shameful, either with another 12 or by yourself; and above all, feel shame before yourself.

For the man who has learned to feel shame before himself, and who, neither in solitude nor in company, will tolerate the doing of anything shameful, but who, because of the reason that keeps guard within him, banishes even the very image of such a thing — he is the one who is able now to hear: "let no one by word or deed induce you." For he alone is proof against deception, and in no way easily misled by anyone, who knows his own worth and is neither cajoled by flatteries nor humbled by those who try to frighten him, whether it be enemies or friends who hold out either of these. For in the words "no one" every person is included: father and tyrant, friend and enemy. And the ways of leading astray come about either through words or through deeds: through the words of those who flatter or threaten, and through the deeds of those who hold out gifts or punishments. Against all these, therefore, we must keep the soul walled about with right reason, so that it may be neither wheedled nor enslaved by the pleasant and painful things that in any way befall us from without. For right reason, dwelling within us, sets temperance and courage on either side of the soul as adamantine guards, and so will keep us undeceived both by the flattery of what is agreeable and by the terror of what is fearful; and upon these follows exact justice, which he commanded above that we practise in deed and in word. By this means, then, no one will in any way prevail upon us to let fall a word or to commit a deed that is not in harmony with right reason. For if above all things we feel shame before ourselves, it is clear that no one will appear to us more worthy of reverence, or more to be feared, than ourselves, so as to induce us to say or do anything contrary to what is fitting. For each of these is harmful to the soul; and what is hurtful to the soul is unprofitable to us as well, since we are the soul.

We must, then, understand exactly the words "what is not best for you," referring the pronoun "you" to that which you properly are. If, then, as the verse says, no one, either by deeds or by words, is to lead you astray to do or say anything that is not profitable to you — and you, as we said, are the rational soul — then you will not, if you are wise, tolerate one who does harm to you, who are a rational being. For you are the soul; the body is yours; and external things belong to the body. By this distinction you will both keep the natures unconfused and discover what the human essence is, never supposing that the body or external things are yourself, nor being over-anxious for them as though for yourself, so that you may not be dragged down into love of the body and love of riches. For, in general, while we are ignorant of what we are, we shall be ignorant also of what we ought to care for, and shall care for anything rather than for ourselves, for whom our care ought to come first. For if that which uses the body is the soul, and the body holds the rank of an instrument in relation to it, and all other things were devised for the sake of the instrument, to support its ever-flowing nature, it is clear that our chief and first care ought to be for what rules and is first, and our second care for what is second. Hence the wise man will not neglect even his health: not that he considers the body the principal thing, but he trains it for the needs of the soul, so that it may obey the soul's activities without hindrance; and in the third place he will care for the things that are third, managing external things for the preservation of the instrument. His first care, then — perhaps even his only care — will be for the soul, since the care of the things that come after it tends towards its progress.

Now everything that is contrary to virtue is, as we said, "what is not best for you"; for to whom virtue is profitable, to him what is contrary to it is unprofitable. He therefore advises us to throw about ourselves a rampart that guards the virtues, when he tells us that we must never obey one who tries to lead us away from virtue, by whatever deeds or words he brings to bear his attempt at a persuasion that turns us aside to the worse. For example: let no tyrant, whether holding out promises or making them good in deed, whether alarming you with threats or forcing you with torments; let no friendly face that hides its deceit under the show of intimacy — let none of these lead you away from what is profitable to the soul. And the only things that benefit the soul, as we said, are truth and virtue. You will be proof against deception if, knowing your own essence — what it is and what it naturally resembles — you always take care to become like that, and regard everything that leads you away from that likeness as the greatest loss. For this, as we said, is "what is not best for you": whatever leads you away from likeness to God; since what is "best" for us is what carries us towards such likeness.

What, then, could anyone offer that would be enough to draw us away from likeness to God and from philosophy? The giving of riches, or their taking away? But we have learned with right reason both how to receive these things and how to part with them, and the instability of their possession does not escape us. For what? If this man does not take them from us, will not a thief? And we shall bear their loss nobly at the hands of one who has nothing. Will not a shipwreck carry them off? And how many other ways are there that bring the ruin of riches? For these reasons we shall also make our reckoning in favour of virtue: taking in exchange for riches a voluntary poverty joined with what is noble, divesting ourselves of them for a well-reasoned cause, and purchasing virtue at the price of all the harm that he who tries to move us from it could do us.

But he will bring tortures, and death. The answer to this is ready to hand: that it is not we who shall suffer these things, provided we keep hold of the "we"; it is the body that will be outraged, the body that will die, suffering nothing contrary to its own nature. For by nature it is mortal and divisible and subject to countless sufferings, which any chance disease inflicts more than a tyrant. Why, then, do we flee from what it is not in our power to escape, and do not rather preserve what it is in our power to keep? For what is mortal, condemned by nature to death, we cannot save from death whatever we do; but what is immortal in us (which is the soul, and is ourselves) we can adorn with virtue, if we do not grow faint-hearted before the death with which we are threatened. And if we endure this death for a well-reasoned cause, we shall adorn the necessity of nature with right choice. These, then, are the great things with which one man might threaten another, whether to suffer something or to pay a penalty; but the things within the soul are not enslaved to another, and are free, if we so will — unless, through an immoderate attachment to the body or to external things, we willingly lead our freedom into slavery, selling the good of the soul for a life of a day and for riches. These are the things the present precept teaches us to accomplish in every case, and through them the steadfastness of virtue, and its immunity to being led astray, is sealed. But let us pass on to what follows, which refers to the same doctrine.
XIV · Verses 27–29
27 Deliberate before the deed, lest it turn out foolish; 28 to do and say senseless things is the mark of a wretched man. 29 But do those things that will not grieve you afterward.

Good deliberation begets the virtues, and perfects them, and holds them together, being at once their mother, their nurse and their guardian. For when we consider in quiet in what manner we ought to live, it chooses the beauty of the virtues. And having chosen to contend nobly in all the contests on behalf of virtue, and being now accustomed to the possession of noble things, even amid the turmoil of adverse circumstances it keeps its judgment unimpaired, in no way so dismayed by the disturbances from without as to change its mind and think any other life happy than the one it had reckoned, by itself, to be the most beautiful. Hence the works of good deliberation are three: first, the choice of the best life; second, the practice of what has been chosen; third, the unwavering preservation of what has been rightly practised. Of these, the first is the reasoning that goes before the deed, laying down the principles of our actions; the middle is the reasoning that accompanies the deed, bringing each thing that is done into line with the governing principles; and the third is the reasoning that follows the deed, reckoning up what has been done and judging whether it was done as it should have been.

Through them all the beauty of good deliberation flowers: now conceiving the virtues, now rearing them, and, in the third place, guarding them. So the beginning, the middle and the end of our goods lie in it, and through it alone come to us both release from evils and the perfection of the virtues. For since our nature is rational, and for that reason deliberative, and is brought by its own choice to deliberate well or badly, the life according to nature preserves its essence, while the choice contrary to what ought to be destroys it, so far as that is possible. Now the destruction of an immortal thing is vice, whose mother is lack of deliberation; and this the verse bids us escape, "lest it turn out foolish".

"Foolish" things are wretched and evil things. For to say or do senseless things "is the mark of a wretched man", that is, it belongs to an ill-fated man. But if you deliberate before the deed, you will neither say nor do anything senseless — things over which those answerable to lack of deliberation must needs be grieved. For the unsoundness of a choice is exposed by regret, once experience has shown the harm, just as, conversely, the nobility of good deliberation leads to steadfastness in the choice, displaying its benefit in the very deeds. And the benefit meant is not that of the body, nor that of external things, but that of ourselves, to whom it is enjoined both to deliberate before the deed and to do those things "that will not grieve" us — and by "us" is plainly meant the soul.

For what profit is there in plundering wealth by perjuries, or murders, or any other evil deeds, and in being rich in outward things, while the soul is impoverished of the goods that properly belong to it? And either to be insensible of this, and for that very reason to intensify the evil; or else, dragged by conscience into a sense of what one has done, to be racked in soul and to dread the places of punishment in Hades; and to find as the only cure a flight into non-being — whence it occurs to him to cure evil with evil, consoling his vice with the destruction of the soul, and to condemn himself to nothingness after death, so as to escape the pains of the judgment? For the bad man does not wish his soul to be immortal, lest he remain to suffer punishment. And so he forestalls the judge there, condemning himself to utter death, as though it were fitting that the wicked soul should not even exist. But he, having been carried down into vice by lack of deliberation, naturally pronounces sentence against himself without measure; whereas the judges in Hades, since they make their judgment by the rule of truth, do not judge that the soul ought not to exist, but that it ought not to be wicked. They take pains to moderate its evil, inflicting punishments for the preservation of its nature, and, after the manner of a physician, treating malignant ulcers with the knife and the cautery; and while exacting penalties for faults, they seek to efface wickedness through the soul's repentance — not removing its essence from being, but rather leading it back into being by purging it of the passions that defile it. For the human soul is in danger of being carried down into non-being through its turning aside to what is contrary to nature; but by being recalled to what is according to nature it is led back up to its own essence, and recovers in its purity the being that was wasting away through its admixture with the passions.

Therefore we must try above all not to err, and, having erred, to hasten to justice as to the healing of wickedness, correcting our lack of deliberation with the better help. For since we have fallen from being good, let us at least lay hold of becoming good, receiving the divine correction with a well-disposed regret. And this repentance becomes the beginning of philosophy, the flight from senseless deeds and words, and the first preparation for a life that knows no regret.

For he who deliberates well before his actions does not fall into griefs against his will, nor does he unwittingly lay down principles and premises whose conclusions and outcomes he cannot welcome; rather he always orders the present, reckoning up the chances of whatever may turn out otherwise. Therefore he would neither, through expectation of so-called goods, overlook the truly good, nor, through fear of their opposites, choose to do evil; but with steadfast judgment he squares his own life by the divine rules.

And that you may know that it "is the mark of a wretched man" to do and say senseless things, look at Medea in the tragedy, lamenting her lot. She, without deliberation, betrayed her nearest kin and, from an extravagant passion, gave herself into the hands of a foreign man; then, slighted by him, she thinks she suffers what is unbearable; and from this opinion you hear how she cries out:
Alas! may fire from heaven strike through my head! What gain is there for me in living any longer?

and she goes on to lawless deeds: first senselessly praying that what has happened had not happened; then, madly trying to cure evils with evils, she thinks to blot out the beginning of her lack of deliberation by a worse end, disowning her ill-considered childbearing by the headlong murder of her children. Or, if you wish, behold Homer's Agamemnon, who, paying the penalty for his immoderate anger, cries out with groans:
My heart is not steadfast, but I am distraught; my heart leaps out of my breast, and my shining limbs tremble beneath me.

And the fire of his eyes, formerly kindled by his angry disposition, he now, when his fortunes had turned against him, cooled with showers of tears. For such is every senseless life: falling this way and that into opposite passions, it is hateful in pleasures and pitiable in griefs, rash when confident and abject when afraid; and, in a word, having no share in the noble spirit of good deliberation, it changes its judgment along with fortune.

So that we may not be filled with such tragic scenes, doing and saying senseless things, let us take right reasoning as our guide in all things, fulfilling that saying of Socrates: "I am one who can obey nothing of mine except the reason which, when I reflect, appears to me to be right." Now all that has been given for the service of the rational being — such as anger, desire, sense-perception, and the body itself, which has been taken on to serve as an instrument for these powers — is ours, but is not ourselves; and none of these ought we to obey, except, as he says, right reason, that is, the rational part disposed according to nature. For this can also discern what ought to be said and done. And to obey right reason and to obey God are the same thing. For the rational kind, once blessed with its proper illumination, wills those things which the divine law determines; and the soul disposed according to God comes to cast its vote with God, and does whatever it does looking towards the divine and the radiant. But the soul disposed in the contrary way, borne at random and as chance will have it towards the godless and the dark, wanders, having fallen away from the only standard of noble things, intellect and God.

Such and so great are the goods of good deliberation, and the evils of the contrary disposition. Deliberating before the deed, besides its other goods, also cuts away the occasions of conceit, summons us to the acquisition of knowledge, and procures for us the most pleasant life, since it procures the best. This is made clear by the verses that follow.
XV · Verses 30–31
30 Do nothing that you do not understand, but learn 31 what is needful; and so you will lead a most delightful life.

Not setting our hand to what we do not know only keeps us free from error; but being taught the things that contribute to the best life provides us, besides freedom from error, with right action as well. For the awareness of our ignorance cuts away the rashness that springs from conceit, while the possession of knowledge gives our activities freedom from hindrance. Both are noble — to know that we do not know, and to come to know what we do not know; and on them follows a life at once the best and the most pleasant. This is the life that is pure of conceit and full of knowledge; that prides itself on nothing it does not know, but is willing to learn whatever is worth learning.

And those things alone are worth learning which lead us up to likeness to God; which make us deliberate before the deed, "lest it turn out foolish"; which do not let us be led astray by anyone, either by word or by deed; which make us able to discern the differences among the words that fall upon our ears; which persuade us to bear the divine fortunes gently and to heal them, and teach fearlessness of death and poverty, and the practice of justice, and mastery of the belly and of what goes with the belly; which introduce the laws of friendship and the honour due to parents; which point out the reverence owed to the superior classes. These and the like are what the present verse says ought to be learned, and on them follows the most delightful life.

For he who excels in virtue also reaps pleasures that bring no regret, pleasures that imitate the steadfastness of virtue. For every pleasure is by nature the accompaniment of some activity or other: it has no subsistence of its own, but follows upon us as we do this or that. Therefore the worse pleasures follow the baser activities, while pleasures of worth enter in together with the better ones; so that the good man surpasses the bad not only in nobility, but conquers him in pleasure itself — the one thing for whose sake the bad man seems to be drawn into vice. For by as much as one disposition is better than another, by so much is one pleasure more worthy of choice than another. Since, then, the life according to virtue, holding fast to likeness to God, is truly divine, while the life in vice is bestial and godless, it is clear that the pleasure of the good man imitates the divine gladness, following in the train of intellect and God, while the so-called pleasure of the bad man (let the name be granted as common to both) is likened to a bestial and frenzied motion. For pleasures and pains change us; and he who draws from them whence he should, and when, and as much as he should, is happy, while he who does not know their measures is wretched.

Thus, then, the life that is pure of conceit is merely free of error; but the life that is also filled with knowledge acts rightly and is perfect; and this same life is at once the most pleasant and the best. Let us, then, never do what we do not know, and what we do know let us do when it is fitting. For ignorance brings in vice, while knowledge seeks the right moment; for many things that are good become bad by a change of occasion. Let us therefore hear the precept in its order: by holding us back from action it brings us freedom from error, and by urging us to learn not everything, but what we should, it leads us up to the best actions. For acting rightly does not lie in not erring, but in knowing what is needful; and the one is brought about by purification from conceit, the other by the presence of knowledge. And from not erring and from acting rightly, see what will befall you: "and so you will lead a most delightful life".

And what life is this, if not that alone which has gained its pleasure from virtue, in which the good and the pleasant have come together? If, then, we long for the noble, and long also for the pleasant, what would the two be when joined? This, he says: the most delightful life. For he who chooses the pleasant together with the shameful, even if for a little while he is enticed by what pleases, yet on account of the shameful he comes to a painful regret. But he who prefers the noble together with toil, even if for the moment he is weighed down by its unfamiliarity, yet finds the toil lightened by its yoking with the noble, and in the end reaps, besides virtue, a pure pleasure as well. For if something shameful is done with pleasure, the pleasure passes, but the shame remains; but if something noble is done with toil, the toil passes, but the noble remains. From which it necessarily follows that the worst life is the most painful, and the best the most delightful.
So much for these verses. And since the training of the body also has reference to the perfection of the soul, see what he adds next:
XVI · Verses 32–34
32 Nor should you be careless of the body's health, 33 but keep measure in drink and food and exercise; 34 and by measure I mean what will not grieve you.

The mortal body, given to us as an instrument for our life on earth, ought neither to be fattened by immoderate bodily training nor worn down by excessive want; for the one and the other alike become an obstacle, and destroy the use we have of it. Therefore the discourse urges us to care for it moderately, and not to overlook it either when it grows wanton or when it is troubled by diseases; so that, preserved in its natural state, it may without hindrance offer its activities to the soul that governs it, able to be led wherever the soul may lead.

For the soul is the user, and the body is what it uses; and the craftsman must take care of his instrument. For one must not merely wish to use it, but also take all the forethought that is possible, so that it may serve us in good condition. And since its nature is established in continual generation and corruption, and filling and emptying nurse it — now food replenishing what flows away, now exercise removing what is in excess — we must set a measure to the filling by what is taken in and to the emptying by what is discharged. And the measure is the reason that harmonises the state of the body with the discursive activities of the soul, and for that reason takes care of the health befitting the philosopher. This reason, then, will choose such exercises and foods as do not fatten the body to excess, nor make it superior to the intellective motions. For it does not care for a body simply, but for a body that serves thought. Hence it will decline the athletic regimen, as one that tends the body without the soul, and will shun all so-called bodily training, as rising up against the intellective light of the soul. But so much good condition of body as can be of service to the contemplation of the mathematical sciences and to the personal performance of noble actions, this he who has chosen the life of wisdom will procure for himself.

For it is to him that the words are addressed, "and by measure I mean what will not grieve you." Let not the measure of care for the body harm you, he says — you who are a rational soul; you, the guardian of the foregoing precepts, must choose such foods and drinks and exercises as make the body obedient to the exercise of the virtues, such as do not carry the irrational part away into rebellion against the governing reason. And you must make your measuring-out of the care of the body with the greatest attention, since you will be held answerable also for its irrational motions. For "the horse that partakes of vice is heavy" — not absolutely, but when it has not been well reared by its charioteers.

In the measure concerning the body he placed drink before food, because it is harder to guard against, slips down more easily, and more readily disturbs the good condition of the body. For a man may without noticing it drink many times more than the measure, more easily than he could eat it. Exercises are placed third, as correcting the repletion that comes from food and preparing us again to take nourishment healthily. For these two things, as it were, run in a circle and give place to one another: food and exercise, exercise and food. For being well nourished supplies the ability to exercise, and having exercised in due proportion supplies the ability to be nourished to good effect. But the measure of these differs from one person to another, since each one's care of the body tends toward his own particular pursuit. For everyone strives to make the body an instrument of his own choice: the wrestler, of the movements belonging to wrestling; the farmer, of the labours belonging to farming; and one man draws the service of the body to one end, another to another, and adapts it accordingly.

What, then, must the philosopher do? With what end in view will he wish to train the body? And of what will he strive to make it the instrument — or is it not clear that it will be of philosophy and its works? As far, then, as it is possible for the body to become an instrument of practical wisdom, so far he will nourish and train it in every respect, caring for the soul primarily and, for its sake, for the body as well. For he will neither prefer the body to the soul that uses it, nor on the other hand neglect it entirely for the sake of the soul that uses it; but he will take care of it in the order befitting it as an instrument, referring that care to the virtue of the user and to the health of the body. Therefore he will not nourish it from every source, but only from those from which he should. For there are things that ought not to be taken, since they weigh down the body and drag the soul's connate pneuma down toward more material passions; concerning which the discourse says later:
67 But abstain from the foods we spoke of, in the purifications 68 and in the release of the soul, judging each thing.

Such things, then, he will decline altogether; of the things it is permitted to take, he will measure the quantity and the occasion, and, as Hippocrates says, he will take careful account of "season, place and age", and of everything of that kind; not allowing us, without examination, to fill ourselves with what it is permitted to partake of, nor, without discrimination, a young man and an old man to follow the same regimen, or a healthy man and a sick one, or one who is beginning philosophy and one who has reached its summit.

All these things the Pythagorean "measure" has comprised, by the addition of "what will not grieve you." For all that contributes to philosophic well-being in the matter of care for the body he entrusted to this brief phrase; and to what he had said before about the health of the soul he added, "Nor should you be careless of the body's health"; so that there the virtue of the user is taught, and here the preservation of the instrument. Join these, then, to those, and you will find who you are, you to whom the precept is given, and that the measure of the ordering of the body must be such as "will not grieve you": such as will not hinder the philosophic purpose, but will by its cooperation benefit the soul that is travelling toward virtue. He spoke of a measure of drink and food, the discourse forbidding excesses and deficiencies and embracing the mean and the proportionate; and from this the mastery of the belly and of sleep and lust and anger comes about easily. For the measure now spoken of chastens the want of measure in those things, and removes what grieves and drags down the soul that is hastening toward intellect and God. For as it ascends toward intellect the soul must have calm from the passionate motions, and the lower things must be well ordered for it, so that its contemplation of the things above may be undisturbed. This was the measure "that will not grieve you": this is what at once masters the belly and secures the preservation of the instrument — what displays the virtue of the soul and does not ruin the state of the body. For it is also a part of virtue to know how to preserve the instrument and to attune it to philosophic use.

But since the care of the body lies not only in foods and exercises, but it needs many other things as well — clothing, for example, shoes, utensils of every kind, and the house that contains them — and since in these too there is need of the moderate, which banishes both luxury and uncleanness from our whole way of life, he fittingly added:
XVII · Verses 35–38

35 Accustom yourself to a way of life that is clean and unpampered, 36 and guard against doing such things as bring envy. 37 Do not spend out of season, like one ignorant of what is noble, 38 nor be illiberal: measure is best in all things.

Not only in foods and drinks, he says, is measure a fine thing, but in all other things too, as being pure of the faults that arise through excess and deficiency. For in all the things we have mentioned there may be a twofold want of measure: one leading out toward extravagance, the other thrusting us down toward squalor. Each is a blameworthy character and not a philosophic one, nor one that aims at due measure in bodily things. For cleanliness pushed too far is found to be effeminacy and softness, while plainness pushed too far becomes uncleanness and squalor. So that we may suffer neither the former through cleanliness nor the latter through plainness, let us walk in the middle, turning aside from the vices that lie beside each, and making each a corrective of the other: practising a way of life plain in such a way as not to be unclean, and clean in such a way as not to be luxurious. Therefore let us prefer measure in all the provision for the body, choosing clothing that is clean and unpampered, a house likewise clean and unpampered, and wishing to have everything whatever that concerns the body clean and unpampered. For since a rational soul governs the body, it is fitting that everything concerning the body too should be ordered in accordance with the governing reason, which will tolerate neither luxury nor uncleanness, since it reckons that all things must be proportioned to its own dignity.

So that it may not be drawn about toward the acquisition of costly things, it practises what is unpampered; and so that it may not dwell with squalor and material formlessness, it chooses what is clean. For example: clothing not fine-spun, but clean; utensils not of gold or silver, but clean, of materials easily procured; a house not adorned with costly stones, nor elaborated beyond need in beauty and size, but proportioned to the needs of the body, and clean. And in general, throughout the whole way of life, it rejects the luxurious as lying outside need, and approves the clean as best fulfilling need. For a garment, a house and every utensil provide their proper use well when they are proportionate and clean. For what need is there of a great platter for a small portion of food? And what need of a dirty one, which will spoil the food? What need of a large house for those who are going to lie in one corner of it? And what need of an unclean one, which does not provide the use of a dwelling? You will find the same in other things too: what is not clean together with being unpampered is useless on either side. For the moment you overstep the measure of need, you have gone forward into the boundlessness of desire. Therefore let everything in your life be measured by the means that escape the vices lying beside them.

"Accustom yourself," he says, "to a way of life that is clean"; then, seeing the lapse into luxury, he added "unpampered"; and had he said "unpampered" first, he would have seen the lapse into squalor too, and added "clean"; always holding us up from a fall by setting the one against the other, so that from both together our way of life may be manly and befitting a rational animal.

And if we order our life in this way, we shall have another great good that follows from it. For we shall escape the envy that grows upon those who go to excess, since by observing "nothing too much" we do not rouse our fellow citizens against us, so that they now resent us as living in luxury, now blame us as living in squalor, and at one time accuse us as prodigals, at another as niggards. For with all such things there follows, from those who live with us, blame for the want of measure. For this is what "envy" signifies here, so that the saying means: "guard against doing such things as bring envy", that is, such as incur reasonable blame from the many. And what is blameworthy both in reason and in the eyes of the many is, in one's way of life, luxury and squalor, and in the spending of money, prodigality and meanness. Therefore let liberality and due proportion display through all external things the prudent state of the soul, and the measure that is best in all things. For, so far as lies in us, the lover of tranquillity must keep away from what arouses envy, and must not provoke envy like some wild beast, so that he may be free to advance undisturbed in noble things.

We shall pursue a life free from envy by keeping a way of life that is plain and free from squalor, and by turning aside from the conceit of those ignorant of what is noble, from which two evils sprout: spending and sparing of money out of season; of which the one is accused of arrogance, the other of pettiness. Liberality escapes both of these, being a virtue concerned with the giving and taking of money, finding what is due in income and expenditure, and ordering all external things in accordance with right reason. So much has been taught philosophically in the Verses about the best use of the body and of external things, so that through these too the beauty of virtue may shine forth; and he makes the following precept the summation of them all.
XVIII · Verse 39
39 Do those things that will not harm you, and reason before the deed.
He has often used this kind of saying: at one time saying,
But do those things that will not grieve you afterward;
at another,
and by measure I mean what will not grieve you;
and,
let no one by word or deed induce you to do or say what is not best for you.

Here, then, the discourse makes a synopsis and a single summing-up of all these, forbidding the admission of what is harmful and recommending the performance of what is beneficial; and it says that the distinction between them is rightly made by reasoning before the deed what is to be done and what is not to be done. For the time for good deliberation is while actions are still uncommitted. And here again we shall understand "which will not harm you" in the same way as "which will not grieve you afterward", applying the "you" to the true man and the rational being, and to the one who has chosen to philosophise and is eager to acquire likeness to God. And this man is harmed by everything contrary to right reason, everything contrary to the divine law, everything that hinders likeness to God. Such things naturally beset us in our association with those who live with us, and in the management both of the body yoked to us and of the things devised to assist it, which it is customary to call "goods for use" (chrēmata), as being laid out for our use (chreia). The discourse therefore says that the lover of divine goods must be thoroughly on his guard lest he ever be persuaded to do anything that is not best for him, and that he must not gratify the body with things that will grieve himself, nor accept anything harmful to his philosophic impulse, for which he will shortly afterwards repent. For it befits us to thrust all these things away by reasoning beforehand, so that the reckoning-over of what we have done may bring us the sweetest remembrance, which he next bids us make.
XIX · Verses 40–44

40 Do not let sleep come upon your soft eyes 41 before you have reckoned over each deed of the day: 42 “Where did I transgress? What did I do? What duty did I leave undone?” 43 Begin from the first and go through them all; and then, 44 if you have done base things, rebuke yourself; if good things, rejoice.

Having come to this point of the discourse, gather together for me the sense of all the precepts, so that the tribunal within the soul, looking to them as to divine laws, may pass judgment on what has been done well or badly. For how will the reckoning afterward be able to reprove us when we have done base things, and praise us when we have done good ones, unless reasoning beforehand has received certain laws according to which we ought to order our life, and unless the treasury of conscience directs our whole life toward these, as toward a mark? He recommends that such a judgment be made every day, so that by the continuity of memory the unerring accuracy of the judgment may be preserved; and toward evening, when we are turning to sleep, so that at the close of the day's actions we may seat the tribunal of conscience, making the examination of our dispositions a bedtime hymn to God: "Where did I transgress? What did I do? What duty did I leave undone?" For thus we shall measure our own life against the rules handed down to us, joining the judging reason to the legislating intellect.

What, then, does the legislator say? To honour the beings superior by nature, according to their essential rank. To make most account of parents and kinsfolk. To embrace and love good men. To rise above the bodily powers. To feel shame before oneself everywhere. To take care of justice. To know beforehand how perishable are wealth and this ephemeral life. To embrace the lot assigned by divine judgment. To have a spirit befitting God, and to change one's judgment for the better. To practise the love of words that are truly words. To be undeceivable and unenslaved in guarding virtue. To use good deliberation before deeds, from which freedom from regret in one's deeds arises. To be pure of conceit. To pursue the life of knowledge. To reshape the body and external things for the activity of virtue.

These are the ordinances that the legislating intellect lays down for souls; and the reasoning that has received them becomes a sleepless judge of itself, often saying to itself, "Where did I transgress? What did I do? What duty did I leave undone?", and taking up its memory in order, for the sake of virtue. Then, if it finds that it has passed the day in accordance with the rules set before it, it crowns itself with the fruits of divine gladness; but if it catches itself having done something out of tune, it applies the admonitions of repentance to itself, as though they were astringent remedies. That is why he says that sleep must be repelled by the eagerness for this reckoning. And the body will hold out, not being dragged down by the need to sleep, because of the temperate regimen, through which even the necessary passions are ordered under the rule of reasoning. For he says: do not admit sleep "before you have reckoned over each deed of the day."

And what is the reckoning? "Where did I transgress? What did I do? What duty did I leave undone?" For we err in two ways: either by doing what we ought not, which is indicated by "transgress"; or by not doing what we ought, as the very wording states. For idleness in the good is one thing and activity in the shameful another; and the one is blamed for omission, the other for admission. For example: we ought to pray, and ought not to blaspheme; we ought to support our parents, and ought not to insult them. He, then, who does not do the former does not do what he ought, and he who does the latter does what he ought not; though both, in a certain way, amount to the same transgression of the law.

He bids us make the reckoning of the day's deeds in order from the first to the last, omitting none of those in between; this is what is meant by "go through them all". For transposition often misleads the judgment, and through the disorder of memory makes what was badly done easy to excuse. And besides, the recollection of our daily life becomes an exercise in the recalling of our former lives, and a consciousness of our immortality.

And this is remarkable: having said "reckoned over each", he did not go on to add "What have I done rightly? Which of my duties have I performed?", but turned the memory toward what is freer from conceit, making the judgment bear on our faults; and he set as judge the most just and at the same time the most intimate judge — conscience itself and right reason, and each man himself to himself, whom we were taught before to feel shame before most of all. For who can admonish another as well as he can admonish himself? For self-determination, availing itself of the freedom of its nature, shakes off the counsels of others when it does not wish to obey; but reasoning that comes from within must of necessity listen to itself. This is the guardian God has set over us; this is our tutor and teacher. This the discourse now makes judge of the day's deeds, and awaits its verdict, so that it may itself vote itself worthy of approval or rebuke. For when it reads over its actions in memory, as in a register, it then judges, looking to the law as its pattern, and votes itself worthy of honour or dishonour. Such daily attentiveness makes the one who practises it a godlike statue, training him by additions and subtractions toward the beauty of virtue, and, so far as is possible, making him a good man. For it is in this that the discourse has culminated, being about to pass on to the deifying precepts.
XX · Verses 45–48

45 Labour at these things, practise them; these you must love; 46 these will set you in the footsteps of divine virtue — 47 yes, by him who handed down to our soul the Tetraktys, 48 fount of ever-flowing nature.

This is what we were saying in the Introduction too: that practical philosophy makes a man good through the acquisition of the virtues, while contemplative philosophy establishes him in likeness to God by the illumination of intellect and truth; and that, as regards us, the lesser must of necessity come before the greater. For it is easier to bring human life within measure by a well-reasoned use of things than to be wholly transformed in nature — which would come about through a complete turning back to contemplation.

And besides, it is impossible to acquire the truth without disturbance unless our irrational powers have been ordered according to intellect by the moral virtues. For the rational soul, being intermediate between intellect and irrationality, can consort without distraction with the intellect prior to it only when, having become pure of its attachment to the things that come after it, it lays hold of those higher things purely. And it will be pure if it is in no way carried along with irrationality or with the mortal body, but takes care of them as one being takes care of another, different from itself, allotting them only so much attention as the divine law commands — the law which does not allow a man to try to lead himself out of life, but bids him wait until God himself releases us. Such a soul, then, will need a twofold virtue: civic virtue with regard to what is below, which sets the irrationality in order; and contemplative virtue with regard to what is above, which procures its communion with the superior beings.

On the boundary between these two virtues the present verses are set: the one, "Labour at these things, practise them; these you must love," as the proper conclusion of civic virtue; the other, "these will set you in the footsteps of divine virtue," as the most beautiful beginning of contemplative science. For the man who has been freed from the bestial life and has purified himself, as far as he can, from the immoderation of the passions, and has for this reason become, as it were, a man instead of a beast — him the verses that follow promise to make a god instead of a man, so far as it is possible for a man to become a god. That this is the end of contemplative truth is made plain by the Verses themselves, in which, toward the end, the poet adds the most beautiful and loftiest conclusion:
70 And if, leaving the body behind, you come to the free aether, 71 you will be immortal, a god undying, no longer mortal.

That we attain our restoration — which is the same as saying our deification — through virtue practised beforehand and through the truth known upon the basis of it, this sacred discourse declares, as we shall see a little later.

But now let us return once more to the verses before us and consider whether the labour, the practice and the love, applied to the precepts already given, mean anything other than turning the whole soul to the exercise of virtue. For the soul, even taken by itself as rational, has in a certain way three powers: one by which we learn, which is now commanded to "practise" these things; another by which we hold fast what we have learned, which is enjoined to "labour at" them; and another by which we cherish what we have learned and hold fast, which is admonished to "love" them. So, in order that we may have all the powers of the rational soul bent together upon the precepts of the virtues, he requires practice of the power whose nature is to think, labour of the power that preserves what has been thought, and love of the power that loves the beautiful; so that from all of them together the possession of goods that are truly good may come to us, together with an unswerving preservation of them and an affection for them grown one with our nature. On these follows divine hope, bringing in the light of truth, as he himself promises when he says, "these will set you in the footsteps of divine virtue" — that is, these will make you like God through scientific knowledge of beings. For to reckon out the causes of beings, which reside primarily in the Demiurgic God, leads to the summit of the knowledge of God, and together with it enters likeness to God as well. This likeness the discourse calls divine virtue, as being rightly mounted upon the human virtue that precedes it. Let the first verses, then, find their completion in a love that is philosophic and loves the beautiful; and, with this love going before, let knowledge of the truth follow, leading up to likeness with divine virtue, as is shown in the verses that come next.

The necessity of the connection between these is further confirmed by an oath. For that human virtue, rightly acquired, makes its way to the divine likeness is sworn with great earnestness by the very one who at the beginning enjoined, "revere the oath." For he commands us to abstain from swearing about contingent things, whose outcome is uncertain. Such things are both small and changeable; hence it is neither worthy nor safe to swear about them, for it is not in our power to bring them to completion. But about things that are present, necessarily connected and of the greatest moment, swearing is both safe and fitting. For neither could the changeableness of affairs ever trip us up — since the things about which the oath is now sworn are bound to one another by the ordinance of Adrasteia — nor does their lowliness and humbleness refuse the witness of the divine; for truth and virtue are the greatest things not only among men but also among the gods. Further, the oath becomes for him a doctrine: that one ought so to honour the teacher of truth as even to swear by him, if ever it be needed to confirm the doctrines; and not only to say of him, "He himself said it," but also, "these things are so, by him himself."

At the same time, in swearing about the connection of the noblest states of soul, he speaks as a theologian, and declares the tetrad, the fount of the everlasting world-order, to be the same as the Demiurgic God. How is God the tetrad? You will find it clearly so in the Sacred Discourse attributed to Pythagoras, in which God is hymned as the Number of Numbers. For if all beings subsist by his everlasting acts of will, it is clear that the number in each form of beings also depends on their cause, and that the first number is somewhere there; for from there it comes here. Now the bounded interval of number is the decad. For whoever wishes to count further turns back again to one and two and three, and counts a second decad to make up twenty, and a third likewise so as to say thirty, and so on in order, until, having counted the tenth decad, he arrives at a hundred. And again he counts a hundred and ten in the same way. And so, with the interval of the decad coming round in a cycle, he can go on to infinity.

The power of the decad is the tetrad. For before the perfection of the decad, which is unfolded, a unified perfection is seen in the tetrad. For when one adds from the monad up to the tetrad, the whole sum comes to the decad: one, two, three and four make up ten. And the tetrad is the arithmetic mean between the monad and the heptad; for it exceeds and is exceeded by an equal number, falling short of the heptad by three and surpassing the monad by three. Now the properties of the monad and the heptad are most beautiful and excellent. The monad, as the principle of all number, holds together in itself the powers of all numbers; the heptad, as virgin and without a mother, has the dignity of the monad in the second degree. For it is neither generated from any number within the decad — as four from twice two, six from twice three, eight from twice four, nine from three times three, and ten from twice five — nor does it generate any of those within the decad, as two generates four, three generates six and nine, and five generates ten. The tetrad, lying midway between the ungenerated monad and the motherless heptad, has taken in and holds together at once the powers of the generating and the generated numbers, being alone of the numbers within the decad both generated by a number and generating one: for the dyad, doubling itself, generates the tetrad, and the tetrad, taken twice, produces eight. The first appearance of the solid, too, is found in the tetrad. For the point is analogous to the monad and the line to the dyad, since it goes from something to something; the surface belongs to the triad, since the triangle is the most elementary of rectilinear figures; but the solid is proper to the tetrad. For the first pyramid is seen in the tetrad: a triangular base, the three, being laid down, and a vertex, the one, being set upon it. The judging powers among beings, too, are four: intellect, science, opinion and sense-perception; for all beings are judged either by intellect, or by science, or by opinion, or by sense-perception. And, in a word, the tetrad binds together all beings — the number of the elements, of the seasons of the year, of the ages of life, of the forms of community. And there is nothing one can name that does not depend on the Tetraktys as its root and principle. For, as we said, the tetrad is the Demiurge and cause of all things, the intelligible God, cause of the heavenly and sensible god.

Knowledge of this was handed down to the Pythagoreans by Pythagoras himself, by whom the author of these Verses now swears that the perfecting of virtue will lead us up to the illumination of truth. So in this respect too one might say that "revere the oath" is kept specifically for the gods who are ever the same, whereas here the oath is sworn specifically by the teacher who handed down the Tetraktys to us — who was not one of the immortal gods, nor of the heroes by nature, but a man adorned with likeness to God and preserving the divine image for those who came after him. This is why he makes him the one sworn by in matters so great, covertly instilling in his hearers reverence for Pythagoras and showing his worth through the teachings he handed down. And the greatest of these is the knowledge of the demiurgic Tetraktys.

But since the first things have been treated in brief, while the second lie in promise, with a firm and undeceiving hope; and since the hierophant of the Tetraktys has been identified, and what this Tetraktys is has been recalled so far as befits the present discussion — come, let us pass on to what the discourse invites us to proceed to, having first shown with what impulse and preparation, and with what cooperation of the superior beings, one ought to approach these things.

In few words the discourse has sketched everything that contributes to the possession of goods: the self-motion of the soul and the cooperation of God. For even if the choice of noble things is in our power, yet since we have this very power from God, we assuredly need his cooperation and his bringing to completion of what we have chosen. For our own endeavour is like a hand stretched out to receive noble things, while what God contributes is the supply and fount of the giving of goods; the one is naturally fitted to seek out noble things, the other to reveal them to him who seeks rightly; and prayer is the boundary between our seeking and God's giving, holding well to our cause, which both brings us forth into being and perfects us into well-being. For how could anyone receive the good if God did not give it? And how would God, whose nature is to give, give to one who is self-determining in his impulses and does not ask? So, in order that we may neither make our prayer in word alone but strengthen it also by deed, nor trust in our own activity alone but hold fast also to the cooperation that comes from God, and that we may join prayer to work as form to matter — and, to sum up the whole, that we may pray for what we work at and work at what we pray for — he joined the two together and said: "But go to your work, having prayed to the gods to bring it to completion." For we must neither merely be eager for noble things, as though it lay in our own power to act rightly in them even without God's cooperation, nor be content with the bare words of prayer while contributing nothing towards obtaining what we have asked. For in that way we shall practise either a godless virtue (if the expression may be allowed) or an inactive prayer; and of these the one, being godless, destroys the very essence of virtue, while the other, being idle, dissolves the efficacy of prayer. For how will anything be noble that is not done according to the divine rule? And how will what is done according to this rule not wholly need his cooperation in order to come into existence? For virtue is an image of God in the rational soul; and every image needs its paradigm in order to come into being, and it is not enough for the one who acquires it unless he also looks there, to that in likeness to which he is to acquire the noble. Those, then, who strive for active virtue ought to pray, and those who pray ought to work at acquiring it; and this was: to act looking towards the divine and radiant, and to bend ourselves towards philosophy, while holding well to the first cause of goods. For that fount of ever-flowing nature, the Tetraktys, is established as the eternal cause for all things not only of being but also of well-being, having spread its own good through the whole cosmos like a pure and intellective light. And the soul that holds well to it, having scoured itself clean like an eye to sharpen its sight, is roused to prayer by its care for noble things; and again, from the fulfilment it receives in prayer, it intensifies its effort, joining deeds to words and confirming earnest deeds by divine converse. And, finding some things and being illuminated with others, it pursues what it prays for, and prays for what it pursues. Such is the union of endeavour and prayer. What is rightly achieved through both of them, let us hear next.

First he foretells that knowledge of God and theological science will be present to those who have been led in this way, and recognition of all the things that have come to subsist from the sacred Tetraktys, together with their distinction according to kind and their union into one cosmos. For here the word "constitution" signifies their ordering together; "how each thing is distinguished," their difference by species; and "how it is held together," their community by kind. For the kinds of rational beings, being distinct by nature, come together into one community in accordance with this very distinction. For by the fact that some are first, some middle and some last, they are at once distinguished and united. For neither could the first become middle or last, nor the middle first or last, nor the last middle or first; but they remain eternally distinguished by kind within the boundaries set by the Demiurge. And so we understand "how each thing is distinguished". "How each thing is held together" we shall consider in turn, as follows. This universe would not be perfect unless it possessed within itself first, middle and last parts, as beginning, middle and end of the whole system. Nor would the first be first unless middle and last followed them; nor would the middle be what they are called unless extremes lay on either side of them; nor again would the last be last unless first and middle went before them. They therefore bring one another in together for the perfection of the whole. And this was their being "held together" by one another: as different in form, they differ; as parts of one cosmos, they enter in together; and by the very fact of being at once separated and united, they complete the whole constitution and co-ordination of the divine world-order — which, he says, you will know if you become master of the goods spoken of before.

With the mention of the extreme kinds the middle ones come in as well; for he says, "the constitution of immortal gods and mortal men". The first are joined to the last through the middle, and the last are drawn up to the first through the mediation of the good heroes. Such, too, is the order of the rational kinds handed down in the Introduction: first in this cosmos are the immortal gods, next the illustrious heroes, and last the terrestrial daemons, whom he here calls mortal men. How each of these should be understood has already been said in the Introduction; but to gain in addition a scientific knowledge of those whose honour we received beforehand from tradition — this comes about for those who adorn practical virtue with contemplative truth, or who are being transferred from the good condition of a human being to divine virtue. For to know beings in this way, as they were made to subsist by God himself, was to acquire a divine likeness. And since after the incorporeal world-order there lies corporeal nature, which fills out this visible cosmos and is co-ordinated under the governance of the rational beings, he next indicates that the good of natural science will follow for those who advance in due order to the kinds of knowledge.

Nature, moulding the visible cosmos after the divine due measure, has made it everywhere like itself through analogy, in different ways, and has imaged the divine beauty throughout all the forms within the cosmos, now in one way, now in another: so as to give to heaven perpetual motion and to earth stability, each of these carrying away a trace of the divine likeness. And to the heavenly body it allotted the circumference of the universe, to the body about the earth the centre. In a sphere the centre is a principle in one way, and the bound of the containing surface in another. Hence the regions above are adorned with stars and with the intellective living beings that come after them, while the earth has been adorned with plants and with animals that use sensation alone. Between things so far apart man is seen as the mean, a kind of amphibious creature, the last of the beings above and the first of those below. Therefore at one time he associates with the immortals and, by his turning back to intellect, recovers his proper lot; at another he herds with the mortal kinds and, by transgressing the divine laws, falls from the dignity that belongs to him. For as the last of the rational kinds he is not so made as to think always and in the same way — for then he would not be man but god by nature — nor is he able to think always, even if not in the same way — for that would place him in the order of the angels. As it is, he is man, able to be led up to the better by likeness, but by nature inferior to the immortal gods and the illustrious heroes, as to the first and middle kinds within the cosmos. For just as he falls below these by not always thinking, but coming at times to be in ignorance and forgetfulness of his own essence and of the illumination that descends into him from God, so by not remaining always in ignorance he surpasses the irrational animals and plants, and rises in essence above the whole earthly and mortal nature, since he is naturally able to turn back towards God, to efface his forgetfulness by recollection, to recover by instruction what he has lost, and to heal the flight from above by the reverse flight.

It befits human nature, then, being such, to know the constitution of the immortal gods and mortal men, that is, the ordering of the rational kinds; and to know also nature, alike in all things, that is, corporeal being, which from above down to the lowest things has been adorned through analogy and divine reflection; and to know all these things "as is right," that is, as they are disposed by law, as they were made to subsist by God, and in what way they have been ordered by his laws, whether bodies or incorporeals. For "as is right" must be understood as applying in common to both works of making. For we must not, yielding to thoughtless impulses, transfer the worth of things to suit our own opinion; but, following the boundaries of truth, we must know all beings as is right, and as the ordinance of the creation has defined each.

From these two kinds of knowledge — that concerning God's incorporeal work of making and that concerning his corporeal — there blossoms a most beautiful corollary: "neither to hope for what is not to be hoped, nor to have anything escape you." For it is from the essence of things escaping our notice that hoping for what is not to be hoped, and conceiving impossibilities, arise. For instance, if someone who is a man hopes to become one of the immortal gods or of the illustrious heroes, he does not know the boundaries of nature and has not distinguished the first, middle and last among beings. And again, if someone thinks that his own soul dies along with the mortal body, through ignorance of the immortality that belongs to our soul, he expects what he ought not, and what cannot come to pass. Likewise, the one who hopes to put on the body of a beast and become an irrational animal through vice, or even a plant through sluggishness of perception — he too, in the opposite way to those who change the essence of man into the higher kinds, thrusts it down to the lower, being in error and not understanding the unchangeableness of the form that belongs essentially to the human soul. For, remaining always man, it is said to become god or beast according as it acquires virtue or vice in turn; but by nature it is neither, only by a relation of likeness to the one or the other. And in general, he who does not know the worth belonging to each being, but either exceeds it or falls short of it, makes this ignorance the starting-point of empty opinion and of hope for what is not to be hoped. But he who defines each thing within the measures set by the Demiurge, and knows beings as they came to be, and measures his own knowledge by God — he most of all keeps the precept "Follow God," knows that "Measure is best," and attains the hope that cannot be deceived.
