Once the ordering of the incorporeal and corporeal kinds has been rightly understood, it follows that the essence of man too is known exactly: what it is, and to what affections it is subject; and that it stands on the boundary between the beings that never fall into vice and those that are not by nature capable of being raised up to virtue. For this reason it inclines both ways in its relations, at one time living there the intellective life of well-being, at another taking on here the passibility of sense. Hence Heraclitus rightly says that we live their death, and die their life. For man comes down and falls away from the happy region, as Empedocles the Pythagorean says, an exile from God and a wanderer, trusting in raging Strife. But he goes up again and recovers his ancient state, if he flees the things about the earth and "the joyless place", as the same poet says, where are Murder and Wrath and the tribes of other Dooms; and those who fall into it wander in darkness over the meadow of Ruin. The longing of one who flees the meadow of Ruin presses on toward the meadow of Truth: the meadow he left when, in the rush of shedding his wings, he came into an earthly body, "bereft of a blessed life".

With this Plato too agrees. Of the descent he says: "When, being unable to follow, it fails to see, and meeting with some mischance, sheds its wings and falls to the earth, then the law is that it be settled in a mortal animal." And of the ascent he says this: that when a man has mastered by reason the tumultuous and irrational mob of earth and water and air and fire which grew onto him later, he arrives at the form of his former and best state; and then he is also led up to his consort star, having become sound and whole. Sound, by release from the passions, as from so many diseases, which comes about through civic virtue; whole, by the recovery of intellect and knowledge, as of his own proper parts, which is naturally achieved rightly through contemplative truth. And again he shows plainly how, by flight from this world, we must heal the estrangement from the superior beings that has come about, when he defines philosophy as flight from the evils here. For in these words he declares that the passions are congenital to mortals alone: "But it is not possible for evils to perish, nor to be among the gods; they haunt this region and mortal nature of necessity." For to things subject to generation and corruption it belongs, surely, to be capable also of being put into a state contrary to nature; and this is the principle of evils. How one must flee them he adds: "Therefore one must flee from here to there; and flight is likeness to God, so far as is possible for a human being; and likeness is to become just and holy with practical wisdom."

For he who wishes to escape evils must first turn away from mortal nature; for those who are mingled with it cannot avoid being filled, of necessity, with the evils that follow it as well. As, then, our flight from God and the loss of the wings that lifted us upward brought us down into the region of mortals, where evils come in along with them, so the casting off of mortal attachment and the growing of the virtues, like wings, will lead us up to the region pure of evils, to divine well-being. For the essence of man, holding the middle place between the beings that always think God and those that are by nature incapable of ever thinking, goes up to the former and down to the latter; by acquiring or losing intellect it presses by turns toward likeness to God or toward likeness to the beast, because of the amphibious character of its nature.

He, then, who has come to know these things about human essence knows how men have self-chosen sufferings, and how they become wretched and miserable by their own choice. For at one time, though still able to remain there, they are dragged down into generation by the rashness of their impulse; at another, though able to be quickly released from here, they entangle themselves in the excesses of the passions. And this is what was meant by neither seeing nor hearing the good things that are near. "Good things" here are virtue and truth; not seeing that they are near is not being stirred up of oneself to the discovery of what is noble; and not hearing is not giving heed to the teachings of others. For there are two ways of acquiring knowledge: by learning, as through hearing, or by discovery, as through sight. Those, then, are said to have self-chosen sufferings who will neither learn from others nor find out by themselves, having no share in the awareness of goods, and being for this reason wholly useless. For he who neither thinks for himself, nor lays to heart what another says, he in turn is a useless man. But those who have made it their work to learn and to discover about goods, these are they who understand the release from evils, and who by flight from the toils here are resettled in the free aether. But such men are few. For most are bad, overcome by mortal attachment, and harmed in mind by their inclination toward the earth; so that this evil too they have from themselves, because they chose to flee from God and to cut themselves off from his company, in which they were happy while they lived in pure light. For it is the separation from God that "the lot that harms the minds" here signifies. It is impossible either that one who has become bereft of God should not be senseless, or that one who has fallen into senselessness should not be bereft of God. For the senseless man is necessarily godless, and the godless man senseless.

Both, then, since they have not been awakened to the love of noble things, have endless woes, carried like cylinders by their downward-tending actions now into one evil, now into another, and not knowing what to do with themselves, because they meet every turn of fortune without education: now insolent in wealth, now doing mischief in poverty; driven to robbery by strength of body, to blasphemy by weakness and sickness; lamenting if they are childless, and making a large family an occasion for wars and for base gain. To say all in a word, there is nothing in life that does not become an occasion of evil to the senseless, hemmed in on every side as they are by self-chosen vice, and by their refusal to look up to the divine light or to give ear to what is truly good; sunk in mortal attachment, they are tossed about in life as in a stormy sea. Of these evils the one release is the turning back to God. It is found by those who awaken the eye and the ear of the soul to the recovery of goods, and who heal, by the uplifting power, the evil that attends our essence.

Now the evil that is at once congenital to us and acquired is the movement of our self-determination contrary to nature, by which we attempt to contend with the divine laws and oppose them, not even perceiving how much we harm ourselves by seeming to resist God, but seeing blindly only this, that we have been able to throw off the rein of his ordinances. And this is what it is to use one's self-determination largely and without measure: to dare to stand apart from God and to take up the baneful strife against him, in which we contend, in a manner, and quarrel with him: when he says, "Do not do this," wanting above all to do that very thing; and again, if he says, "Do this," not doing that very thing; so that those who transgress the divine law fill themselves with misery on both sides, by not doing what is commanded and by doing what is forbidden.

What remedy, then, shall we find against this baneful strife, which is called at once "companion" and "inborn", which is roused from what is in our power when it has been disposed contrary to nature, and which for that reason, as an evil of our own, harms us unawares? What must we set against it? What cure is to be found for raging Strife? What barrier against the power that drags us down, other than to labour at these things, to practise them and to love them, the things that "will set us in the footsteps of divine virtue"? For these were the release from evils which the few understand; these the hearing and sight of the good things that are near; these the deliverance from self-chosen sufferings; these the cutting short of the boundlessness of the passions. These, then, would be the escape from godless strife and the salvation of the soul, the purging away of raging Strife and the recall from our exile from God. For we can heal the downward inclination by the uplifting power only if we do not push it further, nor add evils to evils, but, becoming obedient to right reason, flee the baneful strife by the good strife: no longer striving to disobey God, but striving to obey him with all our strength. And this ought not even to be called strife, but obedience persuaded by God, a turning back toward the divine law, and a willing submission, which cuts away the occasions of senseless disobedience.

All these things, I think, are made plain in the verses before us. Self-determined wickedness is shown through "You will know men whose sufferings are self-chosen", men who must be called "wretched" and miserable, because they have been drawn into vice of their own choice. That they are in no way willing to give ear to what is noble is shown by the words "who, though good things are near, neither see nor hear them". And that it is possible to be released from self-chosen evils is shown by "and few understand the release from evils", which has been set in between so as to show that the release lies among the things in our power, and to make known that the bond hangs upon what is voluntary. Then he adds the cause of the blindness and deafness of the souls that have fallen into vice: "Such is the lot that harms the minds of mortals." For separation from the superior beings leads to senselessness and a choice made without deliberation; this separation he hinted at by the baneful lot which, through our inclination toward the partial and mortal living being, puts us outside the divine chorus. He shows, besides, the consequences of this lack of deliberation, and teaches how faults are at once voluntary and involuntary, by saying that the life of the senseless resembles the motion of a cylinder on a plane, which then moves at once in a circle and in a straight line: in a circle of itself, and in a straight line because of its fall. For as the cylinder, once tilted from the upright, no longer keeps control of its circular revolution about its axis, so the soul too fails to attain the true goods once it has fallen away from right reason and from its conjunction with God; it wanders about apparent goods and is carried off the straight course, rolled about by its attachments to sense. This he expressed by "they roll now here, now there, suffering endless woes."

Since the cause of the lot that harms the mind, and of the separation from divine things, was the movement of self-determination disposed contrary to nature, he taught in the next two lines how this movement too must be lulled to rest and turned back toward God: he pointed out the self-determined harm thus, "For baneful Strife, their inborn companion, harms them unnoticed", and the self-determined cure, "one must not provoke it, but yield and flee." And perceiving that, before all else, we need help from God both to escape evils and to recover goods, he added, as a kind of prayer and a request for aid, the turning back toward Zeus.

It was the custom of the Pythagoreans to honour the maker and father of this universe with the name of Zeus, in its forms Dia and Zēn. For it is right that he through whom (di' hon) being and living (zēn) belong to all things should be named from his activity. For the truly proper name of God is the one that best befits his activities and his works; whereas among us the names that seem proper are assigned by chance and by choice rather than found out through kinship with the essence, as can be seen in many names given inappropriately to certain people: as if a man of wicked character were called Agathon ("Good"), or a man godless in mind Eusebius ("Pious"). Such names have no share in the correctness of names, because they present nothing of the essence or of the activity of the things to which they are given. The true correctness of names, then, must be sought among eternal things; among the eternal, in the divine; and among the divine, in the most excellent. Hence the name of Zeus too is a symbol and image in sound of the demiurgic essence, because those who first gave names to things, through their surpassing wisdom, like excellent sculptors, displayed the powers of things through names as through images. For they made the names in the voice symbols of the thoughts in the soul, and made the thoughts themselves cognitive images of the things thought. Filled with contemplation by turning back toward the intelligibles, and becoming pregnant from there with intellective birth-pangs, they then went forth into speech and gave to beings such names as, by their very sound and by the letters taken up to pronounce them, stamped out, so far as was possible, the forms of the things named, and led those who rightly understood the names back to the essences themselves; so that the end of their contemplation becomes for us a beginning for the discovery of the thought of things. In this way, then, the Demiurge has been named by them, of old the Tetraktys, and now Father Zeus, for the reasons we have given.

And he determines that upon such a turning back toward ourselves there necessarily follow both the escape from evils and the manifestation of what God holds out to us for happiness. The argument, then, proceeds from a hypothesis: that if all were to see what they are, and what daemon they make use of, all would be released from evils. But this is impossible. For it cannot be that all together should philosophise, and receive the goods that God always offers for the perfection of well-being. What, then, remains but for those only to take courage who apply themselves to the science that reveals the goods proper to us? For these alone will be released from the evils fastened upon mortal nature, since they alone have turned back toward the contemplation of the true goods; and these it is fitting to enrol in the divine race, as having been taught by sacred Nature, that is, by philosophy, and trained in their duties. Whether we have any share in the fellowship of divine men we shall show by holding fast to earnest works and to scientific knowledge; by these alone is the soul of man healed and freed from the toils here, as it is transferred to its divine lot.

In short, then, the sense of the verses before us is this: those who have come to know themselves are released from mortal passibility. Why, then, are not all released, since all have within them innate starting-points for the knowledge of their own essence? Because most, as I said, are men whose sufferings are self-chosen, who, though good things are near, neither see nor hear them. Few are those who understand the release from evils through knowing what daemon they make use of; and these are the men who are purified by philosophy of the passions of irrationality, and are set free from the places here as from prisons.

Why, then, does he say to Zeus, "surely you would free all men from many evils, if you showed to all what daemon they make use of"? Is it as though it lay with him to turn all men to the truth even against their will, but through neglect or malice he does not do it, so that they may be held in their bonds? Surely it is not even holy to think so. Rather, the passage teaches this: that whoever presses on toward well-being must turn back to God as to his father. For God is the Demiurge of all things, but of the good he is also the father. So the man who understands the release from evils, who is being freed from self-chosen sufferings, and who cuts off baneful Strife by voluntary flight, turns back toward the everlasting help that comes down from God and cries out, "Father Zeus", calling God father because he has already performed beforehand the part of a son; and he reflects that if what is happening in his own case were to happen for all, all would be released from evils just as he is. Then, finding that this does not come to pass — not because of God, but because of the majority, whose sufferings are self-chosen — he says to himself, "But take courage", as one who has found the way of release from evils. And this way was the turning back, through sacred philosophy, toward the things shown by God, which the many do not see, because they do not rightly use the common notions which the Demiurge implanted in the rational race for the knowledge of himself.

Since, then, to show anything to anyone implies the activities of two persons converging on the same point (for how could you show something to a blind man, even if you held out to him ten thousand times what you wish to show? or how could you show anything to one who sees, if you held nothing out?), both must be present: the good held out by the one who shows, and the discerning eye of the one to whom it is shown; so that the visible on the one side and the sight on the other may converge to complete the showing. This being so, let us take as a hypothesis that all would be released from evils together, if the Demiurge showed to all and made manifest to them the knowledge of their own essence, and what daemon they make use of. But in fact not all are released from evils together. Therefore he does not show to all, but only to those who of their own accord have set out toward release from evils, and have lifted up their own eye to behold and receive what is shown. Therefore he himself is not the cause of his not showing to all; the cause is those who, though good things are near, neither see nor hear, and who for this reason are said to have self-chosen sufferings. The fault, then, is his who chooses; God is blameless of evils. He always lets goods shine forth upon all, so far as lies in him, yet he does not always show them to all, because in most men the contemplative eye for the goods held out to them is closed, and bends downward, taken up with worse things.

Such an interpretation of the verses before us agrees both with the truth itself and with the sense of the verses above. For if it lies with God to draw men to the truth even against their will, why do we charge them with having self-chosen sufferings? Why do we advise that one must not provoke Strife, but yield and flee? Or why do we enjoin men to bear gently what befalls them and to strive to heal it? For the road to virtue through learning is altogether closed to those who abolish what is in our power. There would be no need to labour, nor to make noble things our study and our love, if it were God's own task to save us from vice and to fill us with the virtues while we contributed nothing of our own. But in that case the cause of the wickedness of the many would be a charge against God. If, however, God is not the cause of evils, as indeed he is both said and is, it is clear that our falling away from goods is our own doing, since, though they are near and lie within us in our natural notions, we neither see nor hear them. And the cause of this blindness and deafness is baneful Strife, a self-chosen harm, which one must not push further, but yield and flee from it, understand the release from evils, and find the turning back to God. For in this way the illumination from God, when our sight runs to meet it, becomes a showing. And the works of this showing are the healing of the soul, its salvation from the toils here, the awareness of divine goods, and fellowship in the Father's commonwealth.

Having said this much beforehand about virtue and truth, having completed the precepts of virtue with the nightly review, and having carried the hopes of truth as far as the healing and salvation of the soul, he next adds what concerns the wing-giving purity of the luminous body, attaching a third kind of philosophy to what has been said.
XXVI · Verses 67–69
67 But abstain from the foods we spoke of, in the purifications 68 and in the release of the soul, judging each thing; and consider all, 69 setting above you, as charioteer, the best judgment.

The rational being came into existence from the Demiurge having a connate body, in such a way that it is neither itself body nor yet without body: it is itself incorporeal, but its whole form is bounded and completed in a body. So it is with the stars: their upper part is incorporeal being and their lower part corporeal; and the sun is the whole made up of the incorporeal and of body — not of two things that were at one time apart and then came together (for then they might also come apart again), but of things created together at once and grown together in an order, so that the one leads and the other follows. So it is also with the rational kinds that come next, the heroic and the human: each hero is a rational soul with a body of light, and man likewise is a rational soul with a connate immortal body. This was the doctrine of the Pythagoreans, which Plato afterwards made plain when he likened every soul, divine and human, to the combined power of a winged team and a charioteer.

For the perfection of the soul, then, we need truth and virtue; and for the purification of our luminous body we need the putting off of material defilements, the reception of the sacred purifications, and the strength that joins us to God and rouses us to our upward flight from here. These are what the present verses teach. They cut away the superfluous defilements of matter by the words "abstain from the foods we spoke of"; they instil the sacred purification and the strength that joins us to God by what they convey in veiled terms when they say "in the purifications and in the release of the soul, judging"; and they have rendered to us, complete and entire, the whole form of the human being by what they add: "setting above you, as charioteer, the best judgment". For this sets before us the whole essence of man and distinguishes the order of the parts within it: the judging part as the one that drives, and the following part as the one that is driven.

For anyone not unacquainted with the Pythagorean symbols can learn from the present verses that, along with the practice of virtue and the recovery of truth, we must also take care of purity in regard to our luminous body, which the Oracles call the "subtle vehicle of the soul". This purification extends even to food and drink and to the whole regimen of our mortal body, in which the luminous body is lodged, breathing life into the soulless body and holding its harmony together. For the immaterial body is a kind of life, and generative of material life, through which our mortal living being is completed — a being composed of irrational life and the material body, and a phantom of the man, who consists of rational being and an immaterial body.

Since, then, we are the man, and the man is what he is by reason of these two, we ought to be purified and perfected in them all, but to observe the manner appropriate to each nature; for each thing has its own purification. Thus, of the rational soul, the purification in respect of its rational part is scientific truth, and in respect of its opinative part deliberative virtue. For since we are by nature fitted to contemplate the things above and to order the things below, we shall need truth for the former and civic virtue for the latter, so that we may become contemplators of what is eternal and doers of what is contingent. And by abiding in both respects within the divine limits, we should escape the storm of irrationality. For it is from irrationality that our rational being must be purified, since in its inclination toward generation it attached itself to this as well. But further, a body which is mortal has grown onto our luminous body: this too must be purified, and freed from its sympathy with that mortal body.

There remains, then, the purification of the psychic body, which must be performed by following the sacred ordinances and the arts of the sacred rites. This purification is in a way more corporeal; that is why it also lays hold of materials of every kind, tending this vital body in every way and actively persuading it to separate from matter and to fly up to the aethereal region, where its first happiness lay in having its station. And everything performed with this in view, if it is done in a manner worthy of the gods and not in the manner of charlatans, is found to accord with the rules of virtue and truth. For the purifications of the rational soul take thought also for the luminous vehicle, so that this too, growing wings along with them, may not stand in the way of the upward journey. Its best growth of wings is the gradual practice of withdrawal from earthly things, habituation to immateriality, and the putting off of whatever defilements it has been filled with through its yoking with the material body. For through these it is in some manner revived, gathers itself together, is filled with divine vigour, and is joined to the intellective perfection of the soul.

How, then, might abstinence from certain foods contribute to these ends? For those who are accustoming themselves to be separated from all mortal things, to abstain wholly, here and now, from some of them — above all from those that gladden the heart and draw the mortal body down toward generation — would be a step on the road to purification. That is why abstinence from certain things was also enjoined in the symbolic precepts: its primary meaning is greater and more universal, but in consequence it also keeps us from the particular thing it names on each occasion. For example: "Do not eat the womb of an animal." Taken as it is spoken, this withdraws us from one single earthly thing, and that the smallest. But if you look into the manifold meaning of the Pythagorean depth, you will be taught, through a single example, abstinence from the whole of generation; and as we shall not take this thing among our foods, so in the purifications of the luminous body we shall practise what is understood from it. Likewise "Do not eat the heart" says primarily that one should not enter into the state of anger, but in consequence it also recommends abstinence from this part of the animal. On the same principle we shall regard "Abstain from carrion" as keeping us, as a whole, from mortal nature, and further also from partaking of flesh that has not been sacrificed and is unhallowed. For it is right to keep both the outward sense of the symbolic admonitions and the meaning understood within; for it is through constant observance of the outward sense that right action in the greater things is practised.

So now too we shall hear the verse as giving us, in the briefest words, the beginnings of the greatest works. "Abstain," it says, "from foods" — which is the same as "keep away from perishable bodies". But since it is not possible at present to abstain from all, it adds "which we spoke of". And it points out where these were spoken of: "in the purifications and in the release of the soul", so that abstinence from foods may take such care of the translucency of the bodily vehicle as befits a soul that is being purified and released from the grip of matter. Over such practice it set the judging reason, which is able to bring the care of the luminous body into harmony with the purity of the soul. That is why it called this the "charioteer judgment", as being by nature set over the good order of the vehicle: "judgment", because it was a power of the rational soul; "charioteer", because it lays hold of the body and governs it. But the seeing eye is ranked above the charioteer. For though the soul is one, yet with the eye, as it were, it contemplates the plain of truth, while with the power analogous to a hand it holds the connate body and turns it back toward itself, so that as a whole it may look toward the divine and acquire the divine likeness.

Such, then, is the general pattern of abstinence, aiming at goods so many and so great. The particulars were handed down in secret in the sacred sayings. Each of these, it is true, enjoined a particular abstinence — for instance, from beans among seeds, from carcasses among animals, and among these by kind, as among fishes to abstain from the erythrinus, and among land animals from another, and from yet another among birds; and finally it forbade certain parts of animals, as not to eat the head nor the heart. Yet in each of these the teaching impressed the perfection of purification: while assigning this or that to bodily abstinence on account of certain natural properties, through each it introduced purification from mortal attachment, and accustomed the man, through all of them, to turn back toward himself, to rise up out of the region of generation and corruption, and to migrate to the Elysian plain and the free aether.

And since they made the advance in abstinence in due order, symbols are found among them that are, as one might suppose, in conflict. For "Abstain from animals" is contrary to "Abstain from the heart" — unless perhaps one says that "Abstain from the heart" was enjoined on beginners, and "from animals" on those already perfect; for partial abstinence is superfluous for those to whom the whole animal was forbidden. Therefore we must pay more than passing attention to the order of ascent which the verses indicate. For it says, "Abstain from foods"; then, as if someone asked "Which?", it answered, "those we spoke of". And again, as if to a second question asking where the Pythagoreans spoke of these, and in what traditions of their teachings they set forth abstinences from foods, it added, "in the purifications and in the release of the soul" — the purifications coming first and the release following. Now the purifications of the rational soul are the mathematical sciences, and its uplifting release is the dialectical epoptic vision of beings. That is why "in the release of the soul" is expressed in the singular: because this release culminates in one science, whereas mathematics embraces a multitude of sciences.

To what has been properly received for the purification and release of the soul, then, we must also add what corresponds to them for the luminous body. Accordingly, the telestic purifications must accompany the mathematical, and the hieratic uplifting must follow the dialectical release. For these, which properly purify and perfect the pneumatic vehicle of the rational soul, separate it from material lifelessness and prepare it to be fit for communion with pure pneumatic bodies. "For it is not lawful for the impure to touch the pure." Just as, then, it is fitting to adorn the soul with knowledge and virtue, so that it may be able to be with those who are always such, so too the luminous body must be made pure and immaterial, so that it may bear fellowship with the aethereal bodies. For all things are wont to be joined to one another through likeness, while through unlikeness even things near in place are separated.

This is the measure of the most perfect philosophy that the Pythagoreans handed down, proper and proportioned to the perfection of the whole man. For he who takes care of the soul alone and neglects the body does not purify the whole man. And again, he who thinks he should care for the body apart from the soul, or that treatments of the body will contribute something to a soul that is not purified by its own means, commits the same error. But he who proceeds properly by both is perfected as a whole. And in this respect philosophy is joined to the art of sacred rites, as the art concerned with the purification of the luminous body; and if this art is separated from the philosophic intellect, you will find that it no longer has the same power. For of the things that complete our perfection, some the philosophic intellect first discovered, and others the telestic activity introduced along with it, following the philosophic intellect. By telestic activity I mean the power that purifies the luminous body; so that, of philosophy as a whole, the contemplative part leads, as intellect, and the practical follows, as power. And of the practical let us posit two kinds, the civic and the telestic: the one cleansing us of irrationality by means of the virtues, the other cutting away material imaginings by means of the sacred methods. No small example of civic philosophy is the laws laid down in common, and of telestic philosophy, the sacred rites of cities.

The summit of the whole of philosophy is the contemplative intellect; the middle is the civic; and the third is the telestic. The first holds toward the other two the place of the eye, while those after it hold, toward it, the rank of hand and foot; and all three are so linked with one another that any one of them is imperfect and almost useless without the cooperation of the others. Therefore there must come together into one union the science that discovers truth, the power that brings forth virtue, and the power that produces purity, so that the civic work may be accomplished in harmony with the leading intellect, and the sacred work may be shown to be in agreement with both.

This is the goal of the Pythagorean discipline: that we become wholly and entirely winged for the participation of the divine goods, so that, when the hour of death arrives, the athletes of the contests of philosophy, leaving the mortal body on earth and stripping off its nature, may be unencumbered for the heavenly journey. For then, as the teaching declares in the verses that follow, their ancient station is restored to them and they are deified, so far as it is possible for men to become gods.
XXVII · Verses 70–71
70 And if, leaving the body behind, you come to the free aether, 71 you will be immortal, a god undying, no longer mortal.

This is the fairest end of our labours. This, as Plato says, is the great contest and the great hope. This is the most perfect fruit of philosophy; this is the greatest work of the hieratic and telestic art: to bring men into kinship with the truly beautiful and lead them up to it; to release them from the labours here, as from a subterranean cave of material life; to lead them up to the aethereal radiance; and to settle in the Isles of the Blessed those who have journeyed by the ways already described. For to them is reserved also the prize of deification, since it is not lawful for any to come into the race of the gods except one who has acquired truth and virtue in the soul and purity in its pneumatic vehicle. For thus, having become sound and whole, he is restored to the form of his ancient state, having recovered himself through union with right reason, having recognised the whole divine cosmos, and having discovered, so far as is possible for a human being, the Demiurge of this universe. And having become, so far as may be after the purification, what those beings always are who are not by nature apt to fall into generation, he is united by his knowledge with the universe and is led up to God himself. But since he has a connate body, he needs a place in which to be assigned a star-like station, seeking, as it were, a position. The fitting place for such a body would be the region immediately beneath the moon, as being above perishable bodies but below the heavenly ones; and this the Pythagoreans call the "free aether" — "aether", as being an immaterial and everlasting body; "free", as being pure of material affections.

What, then, will he be who arrives there? What else but what the verse says: "you will be an immortal god" — made like the immortal gods spoken of at the beginning of the verses, not an immortal god by nature. For how could that which from some point in time has made progress and advanced to virtue and deification ever be placed on the same footing as those who are such from eternity? The addition makes this clear: to "you will be an immortal god" it added "undying, no longer mortal", so that our deification may be understood as the removal of what is perishable and mortal, since it does not belong to us by nature or by essence, but comes to us through progress and advancement. So this is another kind of gods, who become immortal by ascent and mortal by descent, and who are necessarily inferior even to the good heroes, since the heroes always think God, while these sometimes fall even into ignorance of him. For the third kind, when perfected, would not become superior to the middle kind, or equal to the first; rather, remaining third, it is made like the first kind while subordinate to the middle. For the likeness to the heavenly beings that is brought about in men by relation already pre-exists, more perfectly and more connaturally, in the heroic and middle kinds. And so the one perfection common to all the rational kinds is seen to be likeness to God the Demiurge. This belongs always and invariably to the heavenly beings; always, but not invariably, to the abiding aethereal beings; and neither always nor invariably to the aethereal beings that fall and are by nature apt to live as citizens on earth. If one should make the first and best likeness to God the pattern of the second and third assimilation, or the second the pattern of the third, one would speak rightly. For our aim is not only to be made like God the Demiurge, but also to be made like the best or the middle likeness, as to a rule. And if, falling short of these, we attain such likeness as we are able to attain, we possess this very thing that is according to nature, and in it we reap the perfection of virtue: in neither being ignorant of the measure of our being nor chafing at it. And the highest virtue is to keep within the limits of the demiurgic order, by which all things are distinguished according to their kinds, and to follow the laws of providence, by which all things, according to their proper power, are brought into kinship with the good that is proportioned to them.
Epilogue

Such is the exposition of the Golden Verses that we have made, containing a moderate summary of the Pythagorean doctrines. For we ought neither to confine our account within the brevity of the verses (for then much that is well laid down in them would have gone unnoticed), nor to stretch it to the length of the whole of philosophy (for that would be more than the present discourse admits), but to proportion the measure of our words, as far as possible, to their meaning, unfolding in them only so much of the general doctrines as suited the exposition of the verses. For these verses are nothing other than the most perfect stamp of philosophy, an epitome of its principal doctrines, and an elementary instruction written out by those who had already ascended the divine path for those who came after them. One might truly call them the fairest token of human nobility — not the record of any single Pythagorean, but the common utterance of the whole sacred company and, as they themselves would say, of the entire fellowship of hearers.

That is why it was their law, every morning on rising and every evening when about to turn to sleep, to listen to these verses as to Pythagorean ordinances, one of them reading them aloud, so that by continual practice of such words they might make the doctrines living in themselves. This we too ought to do, that we may at last, late though it be, gain a perception of the benefit that comes from them.
